subtopic: INSTALLATION' AT INTERNATIONAL BOUNDARY- QUESTION OF INSCRIPTION ON LARGE BELL
INSTALLATION' AT INTERNATIONAL BOUNDARY- QUESTION OF INSCRIPTION ON LARGE BELL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. On Friday evening the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) attempted in committee of the whole to raise a question of privilege with regard to the inscription on the large bell of a carillon being installed at Niagara Falls by the Niagara Falls bridge commission. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) referred, and the press has also referred, to the statement that three ministers of the crown were involved.
1 was one of the ministers concerned, and I have no apology to make for what I have done. The inscription on the bell came to the attention of the federal government as a result of an application by the secretary of the Niagara Falls bridge commission for remission of customs duty on the bells, which were cast in England. The inscription is headed with the name "Churchill" in capitals. The name is followed by a verse which I shall not read. Then come the words:
To God's glory and in grateful memory of our nation's leaders, Winston Spencer Churchill and Franklin Delano Roosevelt.
Hon, members will note the expression "our nation's leaders". Remember that this bell is being installed on the international boundary' between Canada and the United States, not between Britain and the United States. The purpose of the inscription at once becomes obvious. It is clearly intended as an affront
to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King). Surely it is equally an affront to Canada to suggest that our country has to seek its leaders outside its own boundaries.
I did what I believe any other real Canadian would have done in the circumstances. Together with my colleagues from Ontario we drew the attention of two of the Canadian members of the bridge commission to the impropriety' of such an inscription in Canada. The members of the commission in question were Mr. A. J. Haines, the chairman, and Mr. Ross Harstone. I have here a statement from the chairman of the commission as to what followed. Mr. Haines' statement reads:
Mr. Harstone and I were both extremely indignant on learning of the inscription which had been placed on the great bell of the carillon. The inscription in question had been placed there apparently on the sole responsibility of Mr. T. B. McQueston, who, at the time the bells were ordered, was chairman of the commission. The inscription had never been submitted to, much less approved by, the other commissioners.
Our first action was to seek technical advice as to the possibility of removing the inscription without harming the tone of the bell. We learned that this would be possible. I then called a meeting of the commission which was held on Wednesday, June 11, at which it was decided to have all the names removed from the inscription, so that the inscription would read, "To God's glory and in grateful memory of our nation's leaders."
In making this change, no disrespect to anyone is intended and none is involved. Indeed the purpose is to remove disrespect.
Mr. McQueston's statement regarding the technical difficulties and cost of removing th_ names is completely inaccurate. It is surely most unbecoming in one who acted arbitrarily, and without the authority of his colleagues on the commission, in placing the inscription on the bell, to misrepresent the action of the majority of the commission when they are seeking to repair his error.
It will be clear from this statement by Mr. Haines that no pressure was required from federal ministers or anyone else. Once the members of the commission knew the facts, the majority, both of Americans and Canadians, were eager to remove this affront to the Prime Minister of Canada, as well as to other leaders in Canada's war effort, and to Canada as a nation.

PASSPORTS
speechtext:
Why, since when, and in virtue of what authority is an application for a passport considered as a confidential document?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The application for a passport contains statements of a personal nature which are made by the applicant to the department in order to obtain a passport. It
is considered that these statements are made in confidence and are privileged. The information contained in a passport application might, howver, be revealed if there were an overriding public interest in the particular instance. Likewise, information would be divulged to an appropriate inquirer if the person who had made the application has given his consent, or if the circumstances are such that it may be assumed that he would wish to have the particular information revealed to the inquirer, e.g., giving information to the executor of an estate in order that the date of birth of the deceased person may be established for the purpose of payments of life insurance.
It would appear from the records of the department that applications for passports have at all times been considered to be confidential documents.
The issuance of passports is an exercise of the royal prerogative. There is no statutory authority for the issuance of passports in Canada, although there are several orders in council with respect to such matters as the fees to be charged for the issuance and renewal of passports. The royal prerogative is exercised through the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who decides whether information contained in applications for passports shall be made public.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. My question is based on a statement, published in the Ottawa Evening Journal of Saturday June 14, that Hollywood moving picture makers are to come to Ottawa to film the locus and persons involved1 in the recent spy investigation here. May I precede my question by saying that that incident is a blot on the history of Canada, in which it was disclosed that spies, criminals and traitors had infiltrated the public sendee of Canada, and had even come into the membership of this House of Commons, in an endeavour to injure the country. Those found guilty have been sentenced. My question is this. In view of the present tense situation in world conditions does the government consider it advisable to allow that regrettable affair to be capitalized by the makers of sensational movies for the entertainment of the public?
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): Mr. Speaker, the question asks whether the government intends to do something that is not within the powers or the jurisdiction of the government. I certainly do not consider that it is within the domain of the Department of External Affairs to determine what pictures Hollywood interests may or may not make. If they come here and behave as orderly citizens, there is nothing I know of in our legislation which would give any department of the government the right to interfere with their conduct. It seems to be something that their own good taste or their own judgment of their own interests should determine. If the committee now sitting on human rights see fit to recommend to this house that legislation be passed to give some department of government further control over the life and activities of individuals, the house will then have to consider it; but for the time being I would be at a loss to put my finger on any text which would allow my department or any other department of government to take any action about the matter.

subtopic: JAPAN-CONFERENCE OF COMMONWEALTH NATIONS AT CANBERRA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: JAPAN-CONFERENCE OF COMMONWEALTH NATIONS AT CANBERRA
speechtext:
I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. A press dispatch from Washington, dated June 14, indicates that there is to be a British commonwealth meeting on Japanese peace problems at Canberra, Australia, in August. Is Canada to be represented at that meeting? The article also indicates that the United States are prepared to lift the negotiation of a Japanese peace treaty out of the council of foreign ministers and submit it to an eleven-nation peace conference direct. Will the minister tell the house whether such is the case, and could we now have from him a statement of the attitude being taken by the Canadian government in respect of the Japanese peace settlement?

Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): I saw the dispatch to which the hon. member refers, and the writer of the dispatch appears to have more information than the Department of External Affairs. There is under consideration a proposal for a conference of representatives of the commonwealth nations at Canberra. A suggestion had been made that that conference take place early in July. It was not possible for the government of the United Kingdom or for the government of Canada to be represented at that time. Consideration is now being given to the holding of a conference toward the end of August. If that is arranged I have no doubt that Canada will be represented at the conference.
With respect to the second part of the question, the article indicates that the United States is prepared to lift the negotiations of the Japanese peace treaty out of the council of foreign ministers and submit it to an eleven-nation peace conference direct. There has been no official announcement by the United States of any intention to do that. The hon. member knows that there is a commission known as the far eastern commission, which has been sitting in Washington for I think over a year now, dealing with many aspects of matters that will have to be disposed of for the purposes of the peace treaty. There was a suggestion recently that there would be an attempt to avoid the procedure that has given rise to a lot of criticism in connection with the European peace treaties in preparing a draft for the Japan peace settlement. The attitude being taken by the Canadian government is that it would be much more satisfactory to have the eleven nations that have been represented on the far eastern commission represented in the early stages of the preparation of the treaty, so that there might not arise those causes of controversy that have arisen in connection with the preparation of the final drafts of the other treaties.

I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: SCIENTISTS AND TECHNICIANS-PROVISIONS FOR EMPLOYMENT IN CANADIAN INDUSTRY AND UNIVERSITIES
speechtext:
Before coming into the chamber I received notice of the hon. member's intention to ask this question. It was my idea that the matter had been fairly well covered in the press at least, and I thought an order in council dealing with it had been laid on the table. However, I shall be glad, and perhaps it would be a good thing for the record, to make a brief statement in answer to the hon. member's question.
Conditions under which the services of German scientists and technicians might be made available to Canadian industry and universities were indicated in letters forwarded this week to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Manufacturers Association, and educational institutions. It was requested that the specific requirements for individual Germans should be submitted to the Department of Trade and Commerce, which has prepared form contracts in accordance with regulations of the United Kingdom governing the transfer of such nationals. For the employment of German scientists and technicians in Great Britain, a contract must be concluded between the government and the individual concerned, and between the government and the ultimate employer. This system provides for security screening, which has been approved by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The following provisions have been made:
Contracts must be signed by the German scientists or technicians before they leave Germany.
The scientists will be brought to Canada at government expense, which will be recovered from the eventual employer of the individual concerned.
Employment is for an initial period of one year, but may be renewed for a further period of one year. The government is free to return the scientists or technicians at any time.
Payment of salaries will be in accordance with scales prevailing in the United Kingdom, and salaries will be subject to ordinary taxation.
Employers will be responsible for finding suitable accommodation for the scientist or technician, but the German concerned will be required to pay for such accommodation.
Employers will be required to make monthly reports in writing to the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the ability and conduct of the German employee.
The German scientist or technician will not be permitted to write articles for publication
or to give interviews to the press while under contract in Canada without the written consent of the minister.
The emploj'ee will assign to the government, or to whomsoever the minister may designate, his title to all inventions, processes or improvements for which he may be responsible during the period of his contract.
While every effort will be made to employ listed German scientists and technicians for whose services there is an actual need and for whom a request has been received by the Canadian government, no action will be taken to absorb in Canada German scientists for whom no such requirements exist.
At (he present time it does not look as if there will be more than twelve or fifteen such people seeking entry into Canada.

speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement?

Yes. There is no new principle involved in this bill. It is a simple bill which seeks the confirmation of a principle already approved by this parliament. The bill seeks to obtain authority to divert from lake St. Francis, through the Beauharnois power canal, all the surplus water available, subject to prior rights of navigation, for power development.
By section 2, chapter 19, of the statutes of 1931, this parliament granted authority to the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company to divert from lake St. Francis up to but not exceeding 53,072 cubic second feet of water of the flow of the river St. Lawrence, to be returned to lake St. Louis, and in that act it was provided that any additional water which was required by Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power should be authorized by application to this parliament.
By section 1 of chapter 20 of the statutes of 1940 an additional application was made to parliament for 30,000 cubic second feet of water and that too was granted.
Beauharnois Company

The position today is that there is a great shortage of power not only in the area served by Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power but also in the province of Ontario, and this company now comes forward and asks for authority to divert such quantities of wrater of the flow of the river St. Lawrence as the governor in council may from time to time determine, up to but not exceeding all the surplus water of the flow of the said river not required for navigation. In other words, in order to save several applications being made in case additional diversion is required, Beauharnois now seeks, by means of this application, permission to divert all the surplus water available.

Mr. MaeNICOL: I thank the minister for his concise explanation. One thing I like about the Minister of Transport is that he always knows his subject and presents his arguments clearly. In the creation of the world the great architect of the universe, who also was a marvellous engineer, endowed what is now called Canada with vast reservoirs out of which flow many gigantic rivers. Those rivers, through their falls and rapids, have almost inexhaustible power. This bill concerns just a small portion of one of these great rivers, the St. Lawrence, particularly the portion of it which lies between lake St. Francis and lake St. Louis. The distance

between those two lakes is fourteen and a half miles, and in that distance the river falls approximately 83-5 feet. This portion of the river contains three main rapids, and has a large capacity for the production of power. This bill has to do with the production of power from that water.
As the minister has said, this is the third bill which has been before the house having to do with this matter. I remember distinctly the two previous bills, one in 1931 and one in 1940. The fact is that the province of Quebec owns all the power rights in that water. By the law of this land they, owning the river bed, can have possession of all the power which can be produced in that section. The only rights which belong to this parliament are those of navigation. I shall deal with both those aspects of the bill. I am not opposing it in any way; I am for it. In fact, if I might digress for a moment, I should like to say that, when a similar bill was before the house in 1940, I recommended that they be given the full right to divert, if and when they required it all the surplus water. It seems to me that in the meantime the country has lost the opportunity to produce much more power.

That is fine, because that would give them sufficient water to increase their production up to about 1,750,000, more or less. That is a large block of power. In fact the province of Quebec has beent thrice blessed in its very large blocks of potential and actual power energy. First, there is the great power site at Shipshaw. At present in the three plants on the Saguenay we are developing 540,000 and 300,000 and 1,200,000, or roughly 2,000,000 horse-power. I am told that when they conserve the waters of the other rivers which flow into lake St. John, in addition to the present conservation on the Peribonka river, they will be able to produce practically another million horse-power. So far as I know that would be the largest block of horse-power for electrical energy produced anywhere in the world.
In addition they have Shawinigan, which has a large volume. When they take this additional 66,000 feet per second out of the St. Lawrence river it will bring the total up to about 1,750,000 horse-power at Beauharnois.
So that I look forward to a vast expansion of business when all this power is developed and distributed. At the outlet of lake St. Francis the flow of the river is 230,000 cubic feet per second, or thereabouts, depending of course on the flow from higher up in the lakes. In that flow at lake St. Francis there are 5,200 cubic feet per second of water diverted out of the Albany river watershed in Ontario, which, if it followed its natural course, would flow into James bay. However, because of an agreement made some years ago it now flows into lake Superior and down through the St. Lawrence basin. It flows through lake St. Francis.
I have said several times that the fact that approximately 40,000 horse-power can be developed at Beauharnois out of that 5,200 feet which comes from the Albany river watershed is perhaps one of the reasons Quebec has been so generous to Ontario in the matter of power. I wish to thank Quebec for its generosity to Ontario in this respect. I believe they are now selling us 250,000 horse-power out of Beauharnois; is that correct?

I hope they will continue that policy when all the river is diverted through Beauharnois. After all, the watershed behind lake St. Francis is about 230,000 square miles, of which roughly
115.000	are in the United States, and the other
115.000	are in Ontario. In reality one-half of all the water which will flow through Beauharnois will come from Ontario, so it is quite right that Quebec, in her generosity, should let us buy from that power.
I am not going to go much further in the matter. I have a warm feeling for the minister, because he looks into these matters much more than most ministers do. I am not praising him unduly in that regard, but I like the way he makes a study of the work of his department. I suggest that he have a survey made of this watershed, not by a commission, but by his own engineers. The department has most excellent engineers; there are no better to be found anywhere. If they make a survey of the whole watershed perhaps they will be able to give us some good advice. At the present time the watershed is losing some water-not much, it is true. I believe about 3,500 cubic feet per second are taken out at Chicago. They require about 1,500 cubic feet per second for domestic purposes, and they take out about 2,000 cubic feet per second for sewage purposes, street flushing and the like. That is not a great amount of water, and I do not believe it can be reduced.
At Niagara Falls all the water that is diverted at that point flows back into the watershed. I believe even that which goes into the Erie canal flows back through the Lalceport or Erie canal into lake Ontario. So we are not losing anything there. The same applies to the Welland canal. What goes through by DeCew falls through our own power plant goes back into the watershed or into the course of the river. I believe a little water-not very much; perhaps not enough to bother about-is taken out through one or [Mr. McNicol.l
two rivers in Ohio for canal purposes. Then there is a little bit taken out and poured into the headwaters of the Allegheny river. However, all those losses are small. The whole watershed in my judgment has been pretty well safeguarded.
I hope the minister will consider these points. I thought I should mention them in case he is not familiar with them. Of course I am familiar with them, having covered all those areas, having seen them with my own eyes and having noted where these diversions take place.
There have been really only two diversions; I mentioned them a minute ago. I should have said they are from the one watershed, the Albany river watershed. The Kenogami river pours 1,200 cubic feet per second into lake Superior, and through the Nipigon river pours 4,000 cubic feet per second of Ogaki river water into lake Superior. There is a total of 5,200 cubic feet per second from the Albany river watershed. When those diversions came up some years ago I said I hoped that the diversion of 5,200 cubic feet of water per second, which is the equivalent of 500 million tons of water per year, up over a height of land into another watershed, would not upset the whole normal flow of water, and the return of that water in clouds to where the water came from. I am not at all sure that it has not done so. I do not believe anyone can prove that it has or it has not. I have given it most exhaustive study, and the fact is that the great lakes levels have seldom before been as high as they are now. The water today, we are told, is higher in lake Ontario than it has been in seventy years. Toronto island and the cottages all along the lake shore are being severely damaged.
This condition applies all the w'ay up lake Erie. City engineers and other engineers in western Ontario, who have known about my interest in water diversion, have communicated with me about what I said before in the matter, when I pointed out that perhaps at some other time the people living along the shores of the great lakes would have a legal right to sue the governments of the United States and Canada for the destruction of their property through the rising of lake levels on account of this diversion. I do not know, of course, whether the people have that right.
It is a question whether 500 million tons a year poured from one watershed into another might not cause the damage that is being caused today. Certainly there is some cause for it. Perhaps the minister, who I know is interested, might look into that phase of it.

Beauharnois Company
This matter of the flow of air and water is a most interesting study. The diversion of water out of one watershed into another upsets and alters the handiwork' of Divine Providence. Maybe it makes no difference, and maybe it does. That may be the reason for the very heavy precipitation of recent weeks, and may be responsible for the general tendency along this line this year and in previous years. If we could have it in the west rather than in the east it would be beneficial all the way through.
I shall close by asking the minister a few questions. He need not answer now; he may answer when he gets time. We are deciding to allow the Beauharnois Company, or the Quebec power commission, as it is now, to divert all the surplus water beyond what will be used for navigation. That is what it means. As to navigation in the Soulanges canal, I would point out that the Welland and Erie canals take about 3,000 cubic feet per second, but I doubt if the Soulanges canal will take more than 1,000, if that much. If it does not take more than 1,000 cubic feet per second throughout the whole year-the navigation season lasts only eight or nine months-in fact it is immaterial whether it is 1,000 or 2,000 cubic feet, but even if we say that 5,000 cubic feet per second are required, that would leave an average volume of 225,000 cubic feet per second. Through this bill the Beauharnois project is to take the whole of that out. That will mean that not even a rowboat will be able to go down the river from lake St. Francis to lake St. Louis. I do not know whether that is of any importance, because with the Beauharnois canal completed they could go that way and would have a straighter line to sail and through deep water. They would not need to bother going through the five locks there are now in the fourteen and a half mile Soulanges canal between lake St. Louis and lake St. Francis. I just want to see whether the minister and his officers have made sure that at no time will the river bed itself be used for navigation from lake St, Francis to lake St. Louis. That is question No. 1.
Has the United States any rights? In reading up the whole question of diversion from the St. Lawrence I found that just a few years ago the President of the United States appointed a commission with instruction to ascertain the best routes of navigation from the great lakes to the ocean as far as the United States was concerned. That commission was given five references to inquire into, one being the possibility of diverting from lake St. Francis across Quebec and New York to lake Champlain, a distance of about 52 miles, during the course 83166-268
of which the canal would drop about 53 feet. My opinion is that that could not be done, but if it could be done I think it is worth while for the minister to know about it. I am sure he does know about it. The 5,000 feet per second which might be taken at any future time would then reduce our power production at Beauharnois by roughly 40,000 horse-power. I do not think we need worry about that, but it is worth mentioning.
I do hope that the Quebec government will continue to be generous and allow the Ontario government through the Ontario hydro-I believe they are very friendly-to purchase on the present basis one-half of the full production at Beauharnois. We need power very much in eastern Ontario.
I could not find the passage in Hansard, but I remember asking when the 1940 bill went through if diversion works were to be built at the head of the river. I presume they will now be right at the head of the river. Will these be built by the Quebec power commission? The answer to my question at that time was yes.

We were all interested in what the President of the United States said a few days ago. I believe the answers given me in 1931 or 1940 were that any navigation works that were built would be built by the Beauharnois Company. They would have to deepen the 3,000 foot channel to 27 feet, and make locks at Meloeheville where the ships go down to lake St. Louis. I should like the minister to reassure us that that will be done, because we are now giving all the water to the commission.
When the minister gets the time I hope that he will have a survey made into the wonderful possibilities of power production along the whole 1,800 miles of this river. In my judgment there is nothing that we can do that wmuld provide as great a return in jobs as to develop these possibilities. First, there is the work entailed in building the canal. Second, there is the building of transmission lines and so on. Third, there are the hundreds of thousands

of jobs that would be provided in factories all across Canada. There is nothing in the world that will encourage production in a plant to the extent that cheap power will. I would ask the minister to extend his survey in an effort to find some way whereby the maritime provinces and Saskatchewan may enter the cheap power field. These provinces are badly handicapped by lack of cheap power. There is no hope of their greatly expanding their manufacturing potentialities, as we all would like to see them expanded, without cheap power. That would help everywhere in Canada. I ask the minister to see what his officials can do toward providing cheap power for the maritimes and Saskatchewan.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall detain the committee only a few minutes in connection with this bill. Unfortunately there are only three more than a quorum present to discuss one of the most important matters on the North American continent, namely, the St. Lawrence waterway and the cheap light and power movement. I have been a pioneer in connection with this bill. I have tried to prevent the stealing of power by private ownership all over the great lakes. The foundation for this particular company was laid in 1927 when two or three bills were introduced.
I am opposed to the method and manner of bringing up this matter. The Navigable Waters Protection Act was passed shortly after confederation to preserve water powers, inteprovincial and international, on the great system of inland waterways which we have in this country. That act was always under the administration of the Minister of Public Works, but it has been transferred. We find that this bill was introduced in the senate. There are only nine government members present today, six Conservatives, five C.C.F., two Social Credit and one Independent. This is one of the matters which in 1929-30 brought the Liberal party into the valley of humiliation, as it was called then. An investigation into the Beauharnois deals was made afterward by the Bennett administration. I had been a pioneer in the cheap light and power movement in Ontario and strongly opposed the original Beauharnois Company and the methods they used to put this over. My opposition to it drove me out of parliament. These people had all along opposed the cheap light and power movement.
You have to follow certain principles with a matter such as this. Why was this bill introduced in the senate? Why is the Navigable Waters Protection Act violated? After all is said and done, this bill was introduced into the senate, not as a government bill but as a private bill, and the speakers were all private

members. After the first Beauharnois scandal some of them had to resign, but I do not want to refer to names. There was a long investigation into it and a change was made after the general election of 1930.
I object to this bill for the following reasons: First, on account of the danger to navigation. Second, it is proposed by the great leader of our great ally who visited us the other day that construction of the St. Lawrence seaway be begun at once. We have to consider the Chicago diversion of waters in connection with the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway. Hon. members will have noticed in the press and in the congressional reports that there are interests which want a second rival canal to the St. Lawrence seaway, using the Mississippi river. Where are we going to be with the St. Lawrence seaway then? There are cycles of high and low water in the great lakes system in this country, and where shall we be with a rival canal in existence. Navigation will be nowhere. Yet navigation is paramount. You cannot take a bucket of water out of the boundary streams if it affects or injures navigation. Water can only be taken out to develop light and power if it is not necessary for navigation.
I object to the principle of this bill. The explanatory notes say that the Beauharnois Company got a charter and constructed the canal and * the works connected with it, and then by chapter 19 of the statutes of 1931 the company was granted the right to divert from lake St. Francis 53,072 cubic second feet of water of the flow of the river St. Lawrence, to be returned to lake St. Louis and to be used for the development of hydro electric power on certain terms and conditions set out in P.C. 504 of March 1, 1932.
Then by chapter 20 of the statutes of 1940 the company was granted the right to divert an additional 30,000 cubic second feet of water from lake St. Francis on terms and conditions set out in P.C. 3210 of July 18, 1940.
The Beauharnois canal and works constructed and designed in accordance with approved plans permit of the development and use of an additional quantity of water for power purposes.
The Beauharnois Light, Heat and Powrer company is now owned by the Quebec Hydro Electric Commission, which also owns Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated and Provincial Light, Heat and Power Company. These two last named companies enjoy power rights on the river St. Lawrence between lake St. Francis and lake St. Louis.

Beauharnois Company
The explanatory notes go on to refer to the demand for power. Yet they are exporting a whole lot of power now. They were allowed to export a certain amount of power during the war to certain munitions manufacturing plants. Are they to be allowed to continue to export power when this country needs power and will need it for many years to come for industrial development in the two central provinces?
The explanatory notes say that the purpose of the bill is to obtain from parliament its approval of the further diversion by the Beauharnois company of such additional quantities of water of the flow of the river St. Lawrence as the governor in council may authorize.
I am opposed to the principle of this bill, which parliament should not pass unless the two central provinces are consulted and consent to it, and even then we should safeguard navigation rights, which are paramount. The Navigable Waters Protection Act is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works, and I see no reason for transferring that jurisdiction without a hearing before the minister and before the railway committee of this house.
We are going to have a rival seaway, as I have already pointed out; are we going to allow this company to export power that is badly needed in Canada by the two central provinces?
I object to the principle of this bill on the ground that it would be adopting a different type of rival seaway through the Mississippi valley. We may not be able to carry out the St. Lawrence seaway project if this diversion goes through, particularly as Chicago is diverting more water for canals and municipal purposes every year, and there is no proper check being made at the present time of that diversion of water. We used to have a debate in this house lasting for three or four days on the Chicago diversion of water, but now there is no reference to it. That diversion should be checked up, especially as we have cycles of a heavy flow of water followed by a scarcity of water on the great lakes system.
Interests in the United States want a rival canal to the St. Lawrence seaway extending right down the Mississippi to the gulf, and they are going to get away with it. There is nobody to stop them. Chicago is getting away with more water than the treaty calls for, and they will do the same thing with the St. Lawrence and the Mississippi seaway; and then where are we going to be? Future generations will pay for this misuse of the water powers of this country. There is nobody 83166-2684
here to stop them now. In the old days when the Conservatives were in power in Toronto our benches here were full. We had 127 members but today we have only five or six listening to this debate. We were the original pioneers in Ontario of public ownership, with cheap light and power for the people.
I believe that this bill should be laid over for a year. There is no demand now for this extra water. The bill should stand over until we know more about the St. Lawrence seaway. It should go first to the railway committee. I can tell you this, that if this bill goes through, it may prove to be the death knell of the whole St. Lawrence seaway proposition. There are shipping interests in this country that do not want the St. Lawrence seaway. They are opposed to it. The ports of Montreal and Quebec have been developed by a large expenditure of money and this great inland waterway should be extended right up to the head of the lakes. Providence blessed us with this great inland water system. You can go up the Amazon river for a thousand miles. If this bill goes through the way it is you can just fold your arms so far as the St. Lawrence seaway is concerned. I warn the house and the country of the danger. The people today are blindfolded. They do not know what is going on, in local affairs, foreign affairs or anything else. But they will soon wake up to the fact that they have been blindfolded and they will be blindfolded and fooled no more. This is a very dangerous bill for the province of Ontario, if it is passed without all due safeguards. Let us wait until we have all the information about the St. Lawrence seaway. The Beauharnois Company was a private company but eventually it is to be a Quebec public ownership enterprise. This seaway business may become a racket unless the necessary safeguards are provided. History always repeats itself in light, power and transportation. Cheap light and power did great things for our province. We could not have had our great industrial development without it. But those who proposed it and brought it forward were ridiculed and blackguarded, but public ownership in Ontario has succeeded and proved a gold mine. I hope the same thing will be true in the province of Quebec.
I have concluded about all that I have to say because I have dealt with the principles of the bill. The next time this bill is up for discussion I do hope that we shall have a larger attendance from Ontario, anyway. I do not know where we would be if we did not have some of these great national policies which the Conservative party launched and
Beauharnois Company

made a success of in that province, including its support of the St. Lawrence waterway.

From the point of view which I wish to express that is a very useful thing.

30,000	cubic second feet from the river. speechtext: Before the bill passes I wish to say one word. I am not opposing the legislation,, and I am in entire agreement with what has been said by my leader, but I should like to ask this question. How is it known that the required water for navigation has been safeguarded? For instance, you may have ships now that have a draught of 30 feet. Five years from now they may have a draught of 36 feet. How do you know that you are going to preserve navigation?

maintopic: BEAUHARNOIS LIGHT, HEAT AND POWER GRANT OP WATER DIVERSION FROM ST. LAWRENCE RIVER
speechtext: I think I can answer that question. In the first place the department provides checks. At the power house at Beauharnois there are engineers who measure the flow once a week, and our own department officials measure it every month. We also maintain at Coteau water level gauges, as we do at Iroquois and at Cornwall, and we know the level of the water every day. The officers read the reports, and also the reports of the water taken by the Beauharnois company or by the Quebec hydro commission, and by means of comparing these two levels are able to see immediately whether they are taking more water than is required. That is one way. There are several other checks. For instance, under agreements which will be drawn, up between the government and the Beauharnois company it will be stipulated upon what terms and conditions this water may be taken. If these terms and conditions are not complied with, penalties are provided.

maintopic: BEAUHARNOIS LIGHT, HEAT AND POWER GRANT OP WATER DIVERSION FROM ST. LAWRENCE RIVER
speechtext: After we have granted the right to divert the water, and, the diversion has taken place, suppose subsequent events should require that large ocean going ships should have much greater draught than they now have. maintopic: BEAUHARNOIS LIGHT, HEAT AND POWER GRANT OP WATER DIVERSION FROM ST. LAWRENCE RIVER

speechtext:
I should like to add a word to what has been said by my colleague, the hon. member for Calgary West. There can be no question that we have fallen far behind the requirements of the country in the matter of grade separation. The grade separation fund has not been augmented in recent years. Of course we realize that works involving grade separations had to be curtailed during the war. But now that the war is over, I suggest that we should raise our sights in the matter of construction of grade separation works.
When the minister spoke on the resolution he indicated that, in addition to this annual vote to the grade crossing fund, by means of this amendment to the Railway Act the government had in contemplation some augmentation of the fund by special grant to provide funds necessary to carry out grade separation at a number of places where surveys by the board of transport commissioners had indicated grade separation needs were well established. I should like to express the hope that there will be no delay in that respect.
The grant involved in the bill before the committee is not adequate to undertake any large-scale programme. There will have to be some further augmentation if we are to make any serious attempt to catch up with the arrears of work. The expansion of road traffic has increased the existing dangers. Along with that, as I pointed out earlier, the work of grade separation has been largely at a standstill in recent years. So that there is a substantial backlog of grade separation work now to be done. That will require augmentation of the fund.

Raihvay Act Amendment
To add to what has been said by my colleague, the hon. member for Calgary West, let me express the hope that the government will not lose any time in furthering this programme and augmenting the fund.
There is, perhaps, one other matter worthy of mention in this connection, and affecting amounts to be voted in respect of railway grade crossings. The point is that for a period of time it has been the tendency of the board of transport commissioners in its decisions to increase the proportion of total cost of any of these works levied against the public purse, rather than against the railways immediately affected. That is another factor which enters into the problem before us and increases the necessity for our thinking in terms of substantial augmentation of this fund to meet a great need.

Apart from that, there have been spent by the provinces and municipalities $15,675,000 as their share toward the elimination of grade crossings; an additional $16,-
397,000	have been paid by the railways, making a total of $43,867,000 provided for the elimination of these crossings. Then, as my hon. friend suggested a moment ago, parliament can grant a special vote for certain projects which may come to the attention of the government and receive approval.
Then, as I said on the resolution, the board of transport commissioners has been asked to make a survey of grade crossings which in the country are in such condition as to require work being undertaken at the earliest possible moment. Just where the report stands, I do not know. When it does come before the government and what action will be taken I am not in a position to say. However I hope that certain priorities may be established, and that the funds will be voted out of the appropriations of the Department of Reconstruction and Supply or, again, perhaps, out of the funds of the Department of Transport, to eliminate such dangerous crossings. First, the hon. member for Durham asked about the quantity of American as opposed to Canadian materials which went into signals at grade crossings and level crossings. The answer is that approximately two-thirds of all materials used in the installation of automatic signals are purchased in the United States. They are not manufactured in Canada. Then the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario asked who carries out the work of grade separation, and whether it was done in each instance by the railways. If the highway authority is a small municipality which has no adequate staff for carrying out the work, the bridge is designed and built by the railway company. Where grade separation involves the construction of a subway to carry the highway under a railroad, the subway is designed and constructed by the railway company.

speechtext:
Hon. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Minister of Transport) moved the second reading of Bill No. 254, to amend the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, 1933.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-Employer-employee agreements.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CANADIAN PACIFIC ACT JURISDICTION OF FEDERAL AUTHORITY OVER RATES OF PAY, HOURS OF WORK, ETC.
speechtext:
I think the committee is entitled to an explanation as to why this bill is being brought forward at this time. The Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways have been experiencing difficulty with their collective agreements across the country. Under section 92, subsection 10, paragraph (a) of the British North America Act, this parliament has jurisdiction over railways connecting a province with any other or -others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of a province.
As the committee knows, the railways have entered into collective agreements covering rates of pay, hours of work and other terms and conditions of employment with their employees. They have run into certain difficulties, because the provinces under property and civil rights have enacted legislation having to do with the same subjects such as rates of pay, hours of work and certain other working conditions. For example, Ontario provides for one week's holidays with pay after the first year of work. Saskatchewan provides for two weeks of holidays after the first year of work. Alberta provides for one week of holidays after the first year of work and two weeks thereafter. In Saskatchewan I think there are some five provincial statutes having to do with labour matters. In Alberta there is similar legislation and also in British Columbia.
What is happening is that when the railways enter into collective agreements with their employees they are face to face with legislation which is different in each of the provinces. In other words, it is not uniform and is creating chaos. The railways simply cannot operate under these conditions. In Saskatchewan the railways were prosecuted by the provincial government for infraction of their labour acts. A stay of prosecution was

Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act
granted pending an application by the railways to the courts for clarification and for a pronouncement by the courts upon the legality of the provincial legislation. The courts decided against the legislation.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CANADIAN PACIFIC ACT JURISDICTION OF FEDERAL AUTHORITY OVER RATES OF PAY, HOURS OF WORK, ETC.
speechtext: Only as far as railway employees are concerned.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CANADIAN PACIFIC ACT JURISDICTION OF FEDERAL AUTHORITY OVER RATES OF PAY, HOURS OF WORK, ETC.
speechtext:
I am dealing only with railway employees. The hon. member is quite right in bringing that forward. Mr. Chairman, I think a word of explanation should be given at this time. This bill seeks the establishment of the Port Alberni harbour commissioners. The Department of Transport, apart from the national harbours board, operates public harbours in two ways: first, under the control of a wharfinger or a harbour master, both of whom are paid fees of office; second, under the control of harbour commissioners, such as is being sought at this time by the port of Alberni.
There are several examples of the latter class of control of ports, such as the Toronto harbour commissioners, the Belleville harbour commissioners, the Trenton harbour commissioners and the city of Hamilton harbour commissioners in Ontario; St. Boniface and Winnipeg in Manitoba, and North Fraser and New Westminster in British Columbia. When the business of a harbour master and a wharfinger expanded to such an extent that the harbour master and/or the wharfinger is unable to cope with the traffic that is offering in the port, then the question arises as to whether or not there should not be another form of control. That is exactly what is happening in the port of Alberni. It is deemed theie that the volume of business is now too great to permit of effective control either by the wharfinger or the harbour master. The wharfinger is on a 24-hour call and has a crane operator and several wharf employees under his direction. The wharf, besides being used for freight in transit, is used for storage of lumber. There are perhaps two or three
Port Alberni Harbour

large companies and possibly a dozen smaller ones handling lumber. This necessarily complicates the routing of traffic and increases the business.
The demand for this sort of legislation has come from the municipal authority. The port of Alberni city council, the Alberni city council and the Alberni and district board of trade have all made representations for a commission such as this to be set up, and that the business of the port be controlled in such a manner that the commissioners will be responsible to someone in authority. There is nothing new about the principle or about the sections set out in this bill. It is a model bill based on the New Westminster bill and the North Fraser bill. I can think of little of any difference between the statute which incorporated those commissioners and the one at present before the committee.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in moving the resolution I propose, first, to review briefly the developments which have led to the present Canadian shipping and shipbuilding position which, in the opinion of the government, makes the establishment of a maritime commission desirable at this time.
During world war I, the historic Canadian shipbuilding industry, which had fallen on hard times with the coming of iron and steel, was revived by being given orders for forty-two merchant ships to be built for the imperial munitions board. Early in 1918 the government of the day decided that cargo ships for Canadian account should also be built, and a programme for the construction of forty-five ships was started. This was subsequently increased by a further eighteen ships, making sixty-three in all.
In January, 1919, the Canadian Government Merchant Marine Limited was formed as a government agency for managing and operating government-owned ships.
The first of these ships was delivered to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine Limited on February 22, 1919, and deliveries were spread over the following three. years until the last ship of the programme was put into service on January 29, 1922.
The entire fleet therefore only commenced to earn revenue after the armistice, and by the time all the ships were in service the postwar boom in shipping was over and freight rates had dropped more than fifty per cent. The cost to build this fleet at the peak of shipyard prices was approximately S80 million.
Maritime Commission

The government held a five and one-half per cent mortgage on the capital cost of each ship, which the ship's earnings were intended to amortize. This had the effect of saddling each ship with very high charges which they were never able to earn. Various recommendations were made from time to time that the costs of the ships should be written down to their new post-war depreciated values; but these recommendations were never given effect to. This arrangement produced a total accrued interest for the whole fleet of over $51 million during its full period of operation, which amount finally had to be written off, together with a total depreciation of over $31 million.
In March, 1923, the sale of twenty-seven of the ships by public tender was authorized, but bidders were few and by 1926 only eighteen ships had been disposed of.
In 1929, seven vessels were transferred to the newly formed Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited.
Between 1932 and 1935, all but ten of the remaining ships were disposed of and, finally, in 1936, the last ten were sold expressly for operation by a private syndicate between Canada, Australia and New Zealand.
The commencement of the second world war in 1939 found Canada with only thirty-five regular ocean-going ships of over 1,600 gross tons on its register, totalling, in all, 241,880 gross tons. Of these, twenty-two were owned either by the Canadian National Steamships (a company which had been created in 1928 principally to take care of our West Indies trade commitments) or by the Imperial Oil Company.
Once more the Canadian shipbuilding industry was revived, but this time on a very much larger scale than in the first great war. At first, building was confined to naval escort vessels, but in the fall of 1940 the building of merchant ships had become a matter of the highest priority for the allied cause and the United Kingdom called upon Canada to build ships.
In April, 1941, Wartime Merchant Shipping, a crown company, was established to deal with this essential building problem and to develop to the fullest possible extent all the shipbuilding resources of the country.
The first batch of ships programmed by this company consisted of ninety vessels of the "North Sands" type (10,000 tons deadweight). It was later arranged that these should be sold at cost price to the United States, which would in turn "lease-lend" them to Britain.
As a result of this, the British government only bought for cash two completed ships of the twenty-six which they had ordered before the lease-lend arrangement was made.

As soon as construction was well under way, the government decided that a proportion of the ships building in Canada should be retained for Canadian operation.
The Park Steamship Company, another crown company, was accordingly formed in March, 1942, to take over the ships allocated for Canadian operation on the government's behalf. This time, however, it was decided that the ships should not be operated directly by the government agency, but should be allocated by it to various private shipping organizations in the country who would manage and operate them on a fee basis. By this means, private operators were given additional experience in the management of ships, whilst the profits earned by the vessels were turned back through the Park company to the treasury to offset the cost of their building.
As a result of this decision, the first "Park" ship went into service all but three years before V-E day and, by carefully controlling the shipbuilding programme, the last "Park" vessel was completed in September, 1945, one [DOT]month after V-J day. This was a very different state of affairs from that which occurred during and after, the first world war.
By the. time that the ninety ships for Lease Lend had been delivered to the United States, arrangements had been completed for the proportion of ships not required by Park Steamships to be "Mutual Aid-ed" to Britain direct by Canada on a nominal charter hire basis.
The Park Steamship Company was responsible only for ships which were turned over.to it by the government. These vessels were recognizable by the suffix "Park" after their original names (except one, Camp Debert which was also a "Park"). In all, Park Steamship Company have been directly responsible for 176 ships.
One ship named Fawkner Park was bought by the mutual aid board direct from Wartime Shipbuilding, lent by them to Australia, and finally sold to an Australian firm. It never came under the Park company.
The 10,000-ton ships built in Canada and turned over to Britain both by American lcnd-lease and later by Canadian mutual aid were named after North American forts, and the word "Fort" was a standard prefix before all their names. In addition to the ninety bought by the United States of America, a total of ninety-eight "Forts" were turned over to Britain, under mutual aid from Canada. These ships were placed on the British registry but Canada retains title to them.
As the war progressed, various developments took place in the shipbuilding field. The original "North Sands" design, which had

Maritime Commission
coal-burning boilers, underwent two modifications. First, the ships were fitted with oilburning water tube boilers, and this type was known as the "Victory" type. Later, ships were again fitted with Scotch burners but adapted to burn either oil or coal as required. These were known as the Canadian type. To overcome the chronic shortage of tankers in 1942, one "North Sands" and twelve "Victory" type ships were converted to carry liquid cargo. Six small tankers were also built and one was created by a conversion.
A smaller type of ship of 4,700 tons deadweight, suitable for carrying cargoes where the depth of water precluded the use of larger ships, was also constructed. A number of this type were chartered from Park Steamship Company by the Canadian mutual aid board for operation by Britain, and proved particularly useful in helping to provide the requisite tonnage for the invasion.
In the later stages of the war, a number of 10,000-ton ships were suitably modified during building for use as "store issuing" ships and "maintenance" ships for the British fleet. These naval auxiliaries were planned for use in operations against Japan in the Pacific. Later still, the construction of two types of small "China coasters" for eventual use in far eastern waters was undertaken, and three 7,500 ton dead-weight 16-knot diesel driven ships were laid down in order to gain experience in the building and operation of a faster type of vessel.
In October, 1943, the government appointed a special committee to investigate and advise upon future Canadian merchant shipping policy. Two important recommendations of this committee were: that merchant ships should be operated in peace time by private enterprise; and that all government machinery dealing with merchant shipping should be coordinated. The first of these recommendations has already been fully implemented. The resolution now before the committee seeks to provide for the second.
Immediately the war was over, the government set about the disposal to private interests of its Park fleet, together with the diesel ships and china coasters under construction. It was provided that, so far as possible, these ships should be sold to Canadian companies for operation under the Canadian flag. There were, however, a certain number of ships which, for various reasons, were not considered likely to be of use to Canada in peace time, and these were offered for sale in the open market. Eleven 10,000-ton converted tankers, one small tanker, seventeen 4,700-ton freighters and one 10,000-ton freighter in damaged condition were sold to foreign interests. Newfoundland also bought one 4,700-tonner. Fifteen of the thirty-five China coasters were also sold to foreign interests as soon as they were completed.
The remaining government-owned merchant ships were offered to Canadian companies on the basis of a special sales formula. This formula for 10,000 and 4,700-ton ships will be found in Hansard for Tuesday, November 20, 1945, at page 2286. One modification was made to the formula then announced, in that the remainder of the purchase price was to be paid in seven equal annual instalments, and not fifteen as originally set out. In addition to these terms, ships purchased by Canadian companies were to be considered as eligible for the double depreciation under the provisions of section 6(1) (n) (ii) of the Income War Tax Act and order in council P.C. 8640 of November 10, 1944. Moreover, an additional special depreciation allowance of thirteen per cent of the cost of the vessels was allowed in the first year of operations.
It was considered that oil-burning vessels would be more in demand by Canadian buyers. As at that time twenty-eight of this type remained amongst the Forts lent to Britain, arrangements were made to exchange these for twenty-eight coal-burnings Parks then on the Canadian register. Just after this exchange was complete, each batch unfortunately suffered one casualty, so that now only twenty-seven ships are on the exchange list. The coalburning Park ships were transferred to British registry, Canada retaining title to them. When the "Forts" arrived in Canada, the Park Steamship Company acted as agents for War Assets Corporation in disposing of them to Canadian companies under the special sales formula, and the ships came on to the Canadian register.
The response of private enterprise to the sales formula offer was most satisfactory, so that, with the exception of the three 4,700-ton ships which are on long-term charter and seven 10,000-ton ships under sales agreement to be delivered to their prospective purchasers upon the termination of their present charters, the Canadian operated government-owned fleet, including the twenty-seven exchanged "Forts", has now been disposed of. This means that six small tankers, 104 10,000-ton vessels and nineteen 4,700-ton vessels are now in the hands of private operators comprising thirty-three different companies registered in Canada.
The three diesel driven ships were sold by War Assets Corporation to the Canadian National Steamship Company. Nineteen China coasters were sold by the corporation to eleven other Canadian companies, and one was taken over by the Department of Trans-
Maritime Commission

port. The terms of sale to Canadian companies under the special sales formula provide that the ships must be operated under Canadian registry, and no application for transfer to any other flag can be made without the written approval of the Canadian government.
Eighty 10,000-ton ships presently under bare boat charter to the United Kingdom, in which are included the twenty-seven exchanged Parks, remain to be eventually disposed of. A total of ninety-eight of the ships were "Mutual Aid-ed" to Britain and, since mutual aid ceased, have been operated by the ministry of transport. In the meantime, the British have bought ten of the ships outright, and seven of the original ninety-eight became casualties. One damaged ship among these ninety-eight was sold by Park Steamships as agents for War Assets to foreign interests.
The remaining eighty will be returned to Canada for disposal as their charters expire. All are to be returned before the end of 1950.
All told, we built, during the war years, a total of 446 merchant vessels in this country. And although I include the forty-two naval issuing and maintenance ships in this total since they had normal merchant ships' hulls and engines, I am not counting the number of naval escort vessels, mine-sweepers, landing craft and tugs which also featured largely in our total war shipbuilding effort. I will now place on Hansard a break-down of these 446 ships. Of this number, 176 vessels were turned over to the Park Steamship Company.

From the above statements hon. members will see that, of our Park fleet, seventy-four per cent of the original cost of its construction should be recovered. Of the non-Park ships, sixty-one per cent should be recovered. In this case, account must be taken of the fact that, up until September 1, 1945, these vessels were on mutual aid to Britain and earned no revenue or hire.
Moreover, this group includes the three diesel-driven ships and the thirty-five China coasters, which were disposed of for other than war purposes as soon as they were completed at prices which were, of necessity, considerably below their construction costs.
In all, we spent a total of $626-9 million on the construction of these fleets for war purposes. We should finally recover approximately $418-9 million or sixty-seven per cent of our expenditure, leaving an estimated net loss of $208 million. Of this loss, $7-3 million, or 3-5 per cent is due to casualties.
I suggest that the government can look with some satisfaction upon its shipbuilding, ship operating, and ship disposal policies during the past-seven years.
We now find ourselves with a considerable merchant navy. A survey made in 1946 by the united maritime consultative council, which has since ceased to exist, credited Canada with
the possession of a total of 1,948,000 gross registered tons of merchant shipping. On the same basis, the United States were credited with 41,078,000 tons; the United Kingdom,
13,441,000	tons; Norway, 2,663,000 tons; with Canada in the fourth position followed by the Netherlands, Sweden, and France in that order, all of which possess more than one million tons.
A more recent survey made in my department on April 1, 1947, showed that Canadian registered ships of over 1,600 gross tons, which is usually taken as a statistical minimum size for an ocean-going ship, amounted to 386 self-propelled ships having a total of 1,667,724 tons. However, of this total, fifty-two large cargo vessels are confined to operating on the great lakes, whilst seventeen more are passenger ships operating in comparatively sheltered waters.
With the consent of the committee, I will now place on Hansard a table showing the result of this survey for the convenience of hon. members.

From the above table it will be seen that our regular ocean-going tonnage today is 982,869 gross tons, compared with 241,880 tons in 1939, or four times as great. This does not include some 560,000 tons on charter to the United Kingdom and temporarily on British registry. When these British boats are returned the Canadian fleet will be six times as great as it was in 1939. Therefore, whether we like it or not, we are now in the merchant shipping business in a big way. Not only that, but we also have a big shipbuilding potential in this country.
The Canadian shipbuilding industry today comprises seventeen major well-equipped shipyards, and there are also a number of smaller ship and boat building concerns. During the peak of our war effort, there were 53,000 men employed on ship building in these major yards alone. Today they have over 16,000 men in their employ and have orders on hand for 122 various ships, which total roughly 300,000 gross tons.
Before the second world war, the normal government supervision, common to all countries, of our privately owned merchant fleet was carried out by the Minister of Transport, who is responsible for the administration of the Canada Shipping Act, 1934. We also had a section in the Department of Trade and Commerce which administered the various steamship subventions voted annually by parliament, and the Department of National Revenue was responsible for licensing ships in the coastal trade under part XIII of the Canada Shipping Act.
War conditions made it necessary to augment these arrangements considerably, and hon. members will recall that, amongst other agencies, the Canadian shipping board1, under trade and commerce, the transport controller, under transport, and the director of merchant seamen, under transport, were set up to cope with the additional problems which arose. Of these, the shipping board and the transport controller's office have since been disbanded.
We now find ourselves in a world where all governments are interested1 in the maintenance of the merchant fleets owned in their respective countries.
The united nations has under consideration the formation of an intergovernmental maritime consultative council. Moreover, a number of important developments in the general conditions of sea service are taking place. Hon. members will recall that on February 28 of this year my colleague the Minister of Labour tabled the texts of conventions and recommendations which were adopted at the mari-

time session of the international labour conference on seafaring conditions held at Seattle in June, 1946. Since then, the British shipowners' and seafarers organizations have agreed upon and introduced a far-reaching scheme providing for virtually continuous employment for merchant seamen. For these and other reasons, the government feels that the time has come to reorganize our peacetime shipping administrative machinery, in order that it may better be able to assist and encourage our shipping and shipbuilding industries to maintain themselves in a healthy and efficient state. The government attaches considerable importance to this objective from both the general economic and the defensive points of view.
There is no question in our minds of trying to support a large merchant navy merely from the point of view of national prestige. We do feel, however, that a merchant navy adequate to our needs should be retained. It should be one of the duties of the proposed organization to keep those needs continually under review and to advise the government upon the general Canadian merchant shipping and shipbuilding situation.
Hon. members are well aware that a merchant navy is basically an industry which, like other industries, has to pay its way if it is to survive. It is, at the same time, a definite part of a nation's defensive armoury, and a considerable factor in a nation's economic structure. The efficiency of such an important industry is therefore a matter which must be of concern to any government.
Inseparably related to the merchant navy is the shipbuilding and repairing industry, which must also be taken into full account.
Finally I would remind the committee that, as a result of our war effort, we have established in this country merchant shipping and shipbuilding industries of considerable size.
The continuation, development, prosperity, and welfare of these enterprises is of national importance, both economically and strategically, and it is for this reason that I move the resolution now before the committee.

I congratulate the minister on the splendid address he has just given on the need for developing a national shipbuild* ing policy. I remember when I first came into the house what the condition of the shipbuilding industry was, not only on our coasts but also on the great lakes and the ocean. In Toronto we spend S30 million in buying up property on the waterfront and in building and developing our harbour and grade separation and waterfront. When I first entered

Maritime Commission
the house there was a proposal similar to this for the creation of a maritime commission, something like the railway commission, to regulate maritime shipping. In connection with that, a contract came up in the house in 1923, which was known as the Peterson contract with weeks of debate here. As I remember it, the maritime commission found that they had little jurisdiction on the ocean at that time.
I should like to mention the large shipping plants and others along lake Ontario and the upper lakes. As you look across the Detroit river to the United States side you can see the magnificent plants standing on the banks of the Detroit river. You can see the great United States steel and shipbuilding plants; you can see steamships built in the plants passing through the Welland canal which cost this country $130 million, and has a tonnage as great as the Suez and Panama.
We are an aquatic people. We have never given waterborne traffic and shipbuilding the recognition which it should have had long ago as a great national industry and a competitor with rails to regulate freight rates in this country. During the war, as the minister has said, 53,000 men worked in seventeen plants. I hope that some of these plants will be established in our harbour because it was one of the pioneers of shipbuilding on the great lakes. I think of the plants in Toronto that carried on shipbuilding during the war. There was a great shipbuilding plant at the foot of Spadina avenue in Toronto. Dominion Shipbuilding built all kinds of warships in the last war. I hope that this industry will be brought back to our city again as one of the pioneer cities in the construction of these boats.
I should like to mention the condition in which shipping found itself between the two wars. During that time, in the house I used to hold up copies of the Times of London, England, and the New York Times, showing that great liners and other large ships were being sold for taxes for $50,000 and $60,000. That was the awful condition in which shipping found itself before the second war broke out. If we are to have a maritime commission it is now time that we did something about it because I do not know what we shall do in six months time. This matter was referred to in the debate which we had on civil aviation. In that debate the minister showed what the British shipping commission had done in developing shipping the world over to help the empire on the seven seas and Canada. The growth of the empire has been due to shipbuilding and the union coal and steel, which made Britain mistress of the seas.
In view of what has happened at Moscow and Paris, and the fact that the conference there has failed utterly and has been postponed for six months to meet in London in November next, we shall need ships next November when the four powers reassemble. Shipping will have to be on a proper bigger basis so that the maximum food production may be sent to Britain, Germany and to other parts of Europe to save us from an awful disaster over there in the British zone and central Europe and provoke a third war. I believe one of the ways to prevent that is to have more Canadian ships available next fall and winter. In the short time that Canada has been building ships in war time she has shown what can be done. It is a marvellous achievement. A few mistakes were made in connection with war shipping, but that is bound to come about in and after any great war. I wish to commend the minister for the fine report he has made to the committee and to support the principle of the bill. This Canadian maritime commission is to exercise certain powers and perform certain duties and functions under the Canada Shipping Act, to administer any steamship subvention voted by parliament and so forth. Various other functions may be added to the commission from time to time. Shipping is a great national industry and we should have had maritime shipping commission established in the country long ago to keep pace with our trading position as the fifth best in the world for a nautical people.

The minister had made an interesting statement with regard to shipbuilding in Canada and the Canadian merchant marine. I am sure we are all happy that the merchant marine is in a better position today than it was before the commencement of the recent war. As the minister spoke, I could not help thinking of the great difficulty we had in persuading him and the government to get started building these merchant ships.
But for the opposition we wrould have been nowhere.

Today I ran across a portion of Hansard of June 14, 1940, which contains my pointed and sincere pleas to the minister to get started on a programme of building merchant ships, and his reply at that time, as reported at page 785 of Hansard, was to this effect:
Whether at a time like this we should divert the productive capacity of Canada to the peacetime operation of building merchant ships is, I think questionable.

It is a great tragedy that Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island were not continued as the great shipbuilding centres they were in the last century.
