speechtext: Hear, hear.
I am speaking now for the maritimes.
I am talking about shipbuilding.
I was speaking of British Columbia and the maritimes-Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am with you.
I do not think the. Minister of Labour is an expert on shipbuilding. He is on nearly everything else-
I know as much about shipbuilding as my hon. friend does.
-but I question his qualifications on this particular subject.
He was in the navy.
He was in the navy twenty-five years ago andi that gives him some authority.
A pretty good navy too.

Another question is this. What authority and what responsibility will the government or this maritime commission be assuming for directing traffic through Canadians ports instead of letting it go through United States ports? Mr. Bengough made a 83166-269J
representation along that line when he spoke to the cabinet in March. He is quoted in this
way:
He also advocated establishment of a maritime commission with authority to divert traffic through Canadian ports, adjust rates, and generally to ensure that this traffic is moved for the benefit of the dominion generally.
By the way, that question of fixing rates is another important one. Is the maritime commission to have anything to do with rates? If it is to function along the lines suggested in my last series of questions I think it can be of great help to Canada. Probably it will be of help in any event, but we would greatly appreciate having the minister give us clarification on the different points I have raised.
It seems to me that my hon. friend is asking for details of the bill. He asks what powers the bill contains. Surely that is material which should be left until the bill is before the house.

I may point out that one great purpose of the resolution stage, from the point of view of parties in opposition, is that we can make suggestions which may then be incorporated in the bill. It is very helpful to us, and I suggest to the government that it would be well to have these questions asked and answered at this particular stage.
The object of the resolution is to discuss the principle.
I hope the bill is not in such iron-clad form that suggestions made now by members of the committee1 are of no value.
Does the Minister of Transport suggest that the statement of the Minister of Reconstruction dealt only with the priniciple of the bill? He started it.
I said no such thing. I said to the hon. gentleman that the object of discussing the resolution is to consider the principle, and that is a fact.
I merely asked whether the hon. gentleman thought the statement of the Minister of Reconstruction followed his formula.
The hon. member heard what I had to say.

If I may continue, the statement I made, did not discuss details of the bill. It discussed the background, showing the necessity for a maritime commission, which I understand, is the purpose of the resolution. If the committee agrees that a maritime commission
Maritime Commission

is necessary and desirable it will certainly pass the resolution and discuss the details of the bill when it has the bill in hand.
We are entitled to know what the commission is to do.
It is to advise the Minister of Transport on matters affecting shipping and shipbuilding.
We are entitled to more details than that.

I suggested that I make my speech when the bill was before the house. Then we could have discussed the bill. In the meantime we are discussing the principle. The question may be asked as to why the bill is being introduced by the Minister of Recon' struction. The reason is that the Park Steamship Company which is at present under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Reconstruction, is carrying out many of the functions which will be those of the maritime commission after it is formed. In other words, it will be looking after the government's interests in the former Park fleet which has now been transferred to private interests.
The question was asked as to whether the maritime commission will deal with harbours. That matter would, of course,'not fall within its jurisdiction. The maritime commission will merely look after ships and all matters affecting ships, but the matter of harbours for ships will be handled separately by the national harbours board, as at present.
It is the intention that the Minister of Transport will transfer to the maritime commission from time to time certain functions which are now being performed by other officers of the minister. It is the intention that the maritime commission will administer all subsidies. It is the intention that all matters affecting shipping will gradually be coordinated through the maritime commission. My hon. friend has suggested that the maritime commission should allocate shipbuilding.
I did not suggest it. I asked if it was the intention that it should,
Well, what does my hon. friend think? Why did he ask the question?
I thought I was asking somebody who knew.

I think I know the answer. It is a strange question for an advocate of private enterprise to ask. The shipyards are owned by private enterprise and the ships are owned by private enterprise. I assume that the private enterpriser who wishes to build a

ship will build it where he pleases. I also presume that, unless the yards are operated efficiently and competitively, they will in time go out of the shipbuilding business. It will be [DOT] the efficient yards which will survive over the years.
My hon. friend has suggested that the work is unevenly distributed at the moment. That is not correct.
I did not hear that.

I said that it has been suggested that certain yards have work and certain other yards have no work. The fact of the matter is that every major shipyard in Canada has all the work which it can do for the next twelve or eighteen months, which is a situation that I hope the maritime commission will be able to maintain over the years as the department of reconstruction has been able to maintain it over the past five or six years.
Is that true of the shipyards in the maritime provinces?
Yes, that is true of the shipyards in the maritime provinces?
Are not many men being laid off in the Halifax shipyards?

No. They are being laid off in the naval dockyard, not at the shipyard.
I am glad to give my hon. friend that information, because I should like to set him right on that point.
I am glad to get that information.

Can the minister give a little more information about that? I think he said there were 122 ships being built at the present time and 16,000 men employed. Of that number, can he tell us how many ships are being built in New Brunswick and how many are being built in Nova Scotia; how many men are being employed in shipbuilding in New Brunswick and how many are being employed in shipbuilding in Nova Scotia?

Living as he does in Saint John where the only major New Brunswick shipyard is located, my hon. friend should be able to tell me that. I cannot tell him offhand. I can tell him how many ships are being built in Port Arthur, which is in my own constituency, and I presume that the hon. member for Vancouver South could tell me how many are being built in Vancouver.

But you are the responsible minister.

Maritime Commission
The minister gave the total number of ships and the total number of men employed, and I thought he would be able to break that down from the information he has.
I will try to give that information when the bill is being discussed. Is there any question I have left unanswered?

I also asked whether the commission would have anything to do with the number of vessels in the merchant marine or the types of vessel, also whether the functions of the commission were to be purely advisory or whether they were to be operational.

The functions of the commission will be as determined by the bill when it is passed by the Minister of Transport. The Minister of Transport will assign such duties to it as he may deem desirable. Certainly one duty of the commission will be to take over the functions which are now being exercised by the Park Steamship Company in the management of Canada's wartime merchant fleet.
Those ships will all have gone out to private industry.

In a short time; over the next
two or three years. As I say, this is a commission under the minister. The minister assigns to it such duties as he may wish to from time to time. I assume that its duties will be both advisory and operational. Certainly it will be its duty to watch Canada's merchant marine in the best interests of the government, to advise the minister when changes in policy may be required from time to time, to recommend such incentives as may be needed to induce private industry to build a different type of ship or to modernize its fleet; and certainly it will be the function of the commission to advise the minister of any steps that should be taken to stimulate shipbuilding in Canada and make it competitive with shipbuilding in other countries. Surely my hon. friend does not wish me to tell him any more about the bill at this stage.
Yes, I have one more question. Is it government policy to subsidize shipbuilding in Canada?
No, not at present.
Is it a fair question to ask how many men will be appointed to this commission?	'
That is a matter of detail in the bill. My hon. friend may be advised that the bill provides for three.

I should like to ask the minister a question which bears directly on the resolution, which reads in part:
Resolved, that it is expedient to present a bill to establish a corporation to be known as the Canadian maritime commission-
The statement made by the minister this evening does not at all enlarge on the corporate aspect of the commission. What has been said by the minister would be perfectly consonant with a commission which has not a corporate character. Will the minister enlarge on that for the information of the committee?

The corporate character of this commission is exactly parallel to that of the national harbours board. It is formed as a corporation so that it may own property. In other words, at the moment the government owns some ninety ships, eighty of which are on lease to the ministry of transport of the United Kingdom, and about ten are on long-term charters to various Canadian enterprises. These ships will be transferred to the maritime commission. If, in future, it is required to undertake shipbuilding for government account the corporate character will be desirable as an efficient method of doing business.

I was interested in the remarks of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply when he said the shipyards in Canada had all the work they could handle for the next eighteen months. Well, certainly nobody is getting nervous from the rattle of rivetting guns in Prince Rupert at the present time. I would like to see eighteen months of work ahead of them at the present time, in that city, and if he could attend to it I would appreciate it.
I look forward to the formation of this maritime commission, but I should like to know if it will administer all the various points that cover seamen who come under all the various departments. Last year I spoke about the conditions of seamen, and when I got on one angle of it I was referred to this minister and on another angle to another minister. Will all the points come under this commission, so that we may know where we stand, as far as seamen and their conditions of work are concerned?
Before this commission is set up, I should like to see the matter put in the hands of a committee, and have the Canada Shipping Act thrown in along with it, so that we can have a really all-round policy formulated.
When the Canada Shipping Act was reviewed, in 1935 I believe it was, both the present Minister of Veterans Affairs and the
Maritime Commission

Minister of Labour objected to the speed at which it went through. I should like to see more time spent on it in a committee as we will be doing with the national labour code which, we understand, is to come before the house shortly. The formulation of an allround maritime policy should be done likewise. The interested parties should be before us.
I hold in my hand a brief from the Canadian shipbuilding and ship repairing association. Some of the headings are most interesting. For instance, they recommend "that Canadian shipbuilding and shipping policies should be controlled through one responsible government authority, and that Canadian shipbuilders be invited to nominate a representative to all government-appointed committees dealing with questions relating to marine transportation". We do not know the individuals who will comprise the commission, but I should like to see labour represented on it.
I wish to go through one or two of the points which are bothering the seamen at the present time. They would like to see the abolition of the advance note system, and the substitution of slopchests on Canadian vessels. They would like to see a definite ruling on cash draws made by seamen on wages due when in port, similar to the practice in the United States. They would like to see crew accommodations on shipboard similar to those of the United States. Then, they recommend the abolition of shipping fees extorted from seamen for signing on and off ships articles of agreement. They would like to see watches, hours of labour, legal holidays and provision for the eight hour day, the same as obtain in the United States. With respect to sick mariners they would like to see a complete revision of section 308 of the Canada Shipping Act which covers sick mariners, and the coverage of all seamen regardless of whether their vessel sails foreign or coastwise. They would like to see a manning scale, under which there would be a declaration of the government on the question of manning scales for all vessels, and requirements, qualifications and regulations as to crews, certificate of service as able seaman, and penalties for undermanning.
At the present time, on the coast for example, a company can hire some stubble jumper and put him on board. He does not know anything about the work at all. One or two might have a lifeboat certificate, but they might be down in the stokehold. Then,

if a boat 'hits a reef those with experience would be valueless below deck and the deck crew helpless because of lack of experience.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

I have been in one or two panics like that, and I would' not want to see any more. I should also like to see duplicate certificates of discharge, to be issued free of charge when originals are lost through shipwreck.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would call the hon. member's attention to the fact that he is not dealing with the resolution before the committee.
What is a stubble jumper?
You should know.
Is that the same as a sod buster?
Along the same lines.

On the point of order, may I point out that only a few minutes ago the minister himself said that this maritime commission is to carry out all the functions now being exercised by the Department of Transport.
No.
With regard to shipping. All the points raised by the hon. member for Skeena are in that category. I submit that he is in order.
A stubble jumper is a C.C.F. name for a farmer.
The hon. member is discussing the Canada Shipping Act.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member is discussing the Canada Shipping Act, which has nothing to do with the resolution before the committee.
Yes, it has. This new commission is to take over certain of the administrative work under the Canada Shipping Act.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: In dealing with a resolution of this kind, the committee can deal only with the principle involved, as to whether or not a commission is to be set up, and what the functions of that commission should be. I believe the hon. member is dealing with something with which, in all probability, this commission will have nothing to do.
What did I say? Quote the words.

These are the words:
Before the second world war, the normal government supervision (common to all countries) of our privately-owned merchant fleet was carried out by the Minister of Transport, who is responsible for the administration of the Canada Shipping Act, 1934.
Then he goes on to deal with the Department of Trade and Commerce, which administers steamship subventions; then, with the Canadian shipping board, the transport controller and the director of merchant seamen. My understanding is that these functions are now to be taken over by the Canadian maritime commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He did not say that.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I should like to see the committee support the Chair sometimes in trying to conduct business in an orderly fashion. I have spent a good deal of time in looking over debates involving problems such as this which have been dealt with by chairmen of committees. I have looked1 into what happened during the first period of time I was here, when Mr. Bennett headed the government. I find that the same rulings were given by chairmen at that time, and that on many occasions hon. members who then sat in opposition were taking the same position as the hon. member for Vancouver South now takes.
After all, a chairman must assume responsibility and give direction to the committee. I believe the committee will make better progress if it tries to support the Chair. I want to be fair to all. But at the same time there are rules by which we should be governed.

May I say a word-and I do so only to assist the Chair, as I conceive it my duty to do. There is one sentence which might have been read from the minister's statement where it deals with merchant shipping. After reviewing the activities of various government agencies, some of which were mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver South, he proceeded to discuss the functions of the proposed maritime commission in this way:
It should be one of the duties of the proposed organization to keep those needs continually under review and to advise the government upon the general Canadian merchant shipping and shipbuilding situation.
I call special attention to the words "general Canadian merchant shipping and shipbuilding situation".

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Question.
Don't be in a hurry.

I had the floor, until someone else jumped up and took it. I did not ask for any help, and I was not fighting with the Chairman, I accept his ruling. The minister did deal at length with the Park Steamship Company. He did not, however, tell about the wages they paid during the war -and they were not so hot. I have brought up the question at this time because I thought I was being constructive. The resolution, as it reads, deals with certain duties, functions and powers. But one has to be a bit of a mind reader to find out what those principles are. If you inject something constructive into it it would be w-orth while.
I would point out, however, that I should like to see this go to a committee of the house where it would be threshed out, and from which might come an all-round shipping policy which would be suitable both to the shipping companies and to labour. It is apt to be too one-sided and we should try to bring peace into an industry which has not been in too steady a state for a number of years.

The resolution and the minister's comments on it are, I think, both highly commendable at the present time. I was particularly pleased when the minister said:
. . . that merchant ships should be operated in peace time by private enterprise and that all government machinery dealing with merchant shipping should be coordinated.
I agree fully with that, I liked also this statement of the minister:
We spent a total of $626-9 million on the construction of these fleets for war purposes.
And also the statement:
Therefore, whether we like it or not, we are now in the merchant shipping business in a big way. Not only that, but we also have a big shipbuilding potential in this country.
Those were good things to say. The minister further said:
I suggest that the government can look with some satisfaction upon its shipbuilding, ship operating and ship disposal policies during the past several years. I think those policies have been thoroughly justified.
Then the minister said:
We now find ourselves in a world where all governments are interested in the maintenance of the merchant fleets owned in their respective countries.
Maritime Commission

The minister indicates there what I consider a most commendable attitude toward the responsibility of Canada in connection with the defence of freedom in the world in the days to come. I wish to congratulate him upon that statement. Then he went on to say:
We do feel, however, that a merchant navy adequate to our needs should be retained. It should be one of the duties of the proposed organization to keep those needs continually under review and to advise the government upon the general Canadian merchant shipping and shipbuilding situation.
And again:
Inseparably related to the merchant navy is the shipbuilding and repairing industry, which must also be taken into full account. Finally ... as a result of our war effort, we have established^ in this country merchant shipping and shipbuilding industries of considerable size.
While the war was on. I had the privilege of travelling around a little bit in connection with the work of the war expenditures committee; I was greatly impressed with the size and1 quality of the shipbuilding industry which had been established in this country. I was genuinely proud; I felt much more happy to be a Canadian after seeing what we were able to do in Canada.
Finally, the minister said:
The continuation, development, prosperity, *and welfare of these enterprises is of national importance, both economically and strategically, and it is for this reason that I move the resolution now before the house.
Those words find a responsive chord in my being; I am glad the minister used them. While it is said to be poor politics for a member of the opposition to congratulate the government upon what they have done, I do not look at the functions of the opposition in that way. I believe that in a democracy when people do a good job everybody should recognize it as a good job and say so frankly. I think in the past war the minister and his colleagues had a tremendous responsibility and I believe they discharged that responsibility well. I think they deserve commendation and I am ready to give my little quota toward rewarding them. I wish to congratulate the minister upon his achievements in the past and upon his attitude toward the future. I want to say also that I believe this setting up of a maritime commission is a right step at the present time. It inidicates that the same skilful and far-seeing mind that guided our work in this respect during the war is still in charge.
I know I do not need to suggest to the minister that there are enormous problems ahead, probably quite comparable with those which he has solved in the past. The cost of the suitable measures which will have to be
[Mr. Blackmore.l
taken in order to attain the objectives which the minister's words clearly indicate he envisages will be a tremendous item for consideration. I hope the house and the country will be ready to support the minister with the financial means he will require.
I should like to express some doubt that he will be able to acomplish all the things which he has envisaged under the present financial system. I do not wish to go into any considerable discussion on that matter because I would be quite out of order at the present time, but I believe that sooner or later we shall have to face up to the fact, and we must adopt a realistic financial system if we are to attain the wide objectives which must be attained in the days immediately ahead. I just throw out that suggestion to the minister so that he may keep it in mind should he have any spare moments in which to consider such matters.
In closing, I should like to urge the minister that he go forward with the vision and energy and effectiveness which have characterized his efforts during the war. Further, I urge him that if he should find himself hampered by the present financial system he should not hesitate to advocate that such changes be made in that system as will enable him to serve Canada first, and not the financial system first.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not trespass upon the rules of the house by attempting to discuss the details of a bill which I have not seen, but it does seem to me that the minister's remarks were largely of an historical character and contained very little about the principles which we might expect to be contained in a bill having to do with the setting up of a maritime commission. What we learned from his remarks was a history of shipping and shipbuilding in Canada and that we are now in the business in a big way, whether we like it or not. Then he said that we must reorganize our shipping administration. I failed to learn very much, either from the document which he circulated or the speech which he made, about the principles to be contained in the bill to be presented to this house.
The minister did say that the merchant navy of Canada under Canadian registry should be adequate to our needs. The word "adequate" is capable of broad and differing interpretations. Before the resolution is carried, I think we should have more enlightenment as to what the minister means by the words "adequate to our needs." It has been the habit in the past for Canada to have a great deal of her foreign trade carried by bottoms of other countries, and in that way those countries were able to pay for, the wheat

Maritime Commission
and other natural and manufactured products which they purchased from Canada.
I come now to a matter of deep principle and concern which I think the minister should have touched upon. I find that the United States maritime commission is made up of five members, and their act contains a provision that not more than three of those members shall be from the same political party. I hope that that comment will rise to the level of a principle in this bill in the eyes of the minister. How long is the term of these commissioners to be? In the United States the terms are staggered. From the inception of the committee the terms were two, three, four, five and six years, and upon retirement of a member the new member is elected for a period of six years. Then the minister has said nothing as to what this commission is to do. Is it to run our ocean services and supervise rates and so on? Is it to deal exclusively writh foreign shipping, or is it to deal also with domestic shipping or shipping which is partly domestic and partly foreign?
The minister mentioned that there would be subsidies or the possibility of subsidies in connection with shipbuilding in this country. May I ask him if there will also be operational subsidies as well as construction subsidies?
Will my hon. friend quote the passage where I said there would be construction subsidies?

1 gathered from the
minister's general remarks that there would be subsidies, but if he indicates to me I was mistaken I shall be glad to withdraw. Shipbuilding, however, is generally conceded to be much more expensive in Canada. If I recall correctly, the cost of the destroyers we built was almost three times as much as in Great Britain, and it is a natural assumption that shipbuilding may cost more in this country. If that is not so I am sure the country will be happy to hear it. Perhaps the minister will explain how private owners of shipping lines will be able to purchase ships built in Canada as cheaply as they can purchase them in Great Britain or in other countries.
Will there be a provision in the bill for the acquisition by the maritime commission of obsolete vessels? In the United States maritime commission act there is a provision whereby vessels seventeen years of age or over which have become obsolete will be taken over by the .commission and funds are made available for ship-owning lines to acquire new ships built in that country.
The minister did not mention anything about insurance. It may be a question of S3166-270
principle whether the government intends to embark on that veiy large and important aspect of the shipping trade, as has been done in the United States.
I think it would also be most useful to the committee to learn something about the intergovernmental maritime consultative council which the minister mentioned in his remarks. Has it been set up, or is it likely to be set up soon, and what is expected of it?
Is it the intention under this bill to have a reserve fleet set up, which would be of great assistance in the event of another war? I might quote from an article in the Yale Review, which says:
The strategic importance of merchant shipping has long been known and ably expressed by many writers from the time of Rear Admiral Mahan on. Admiral Nimitz has recently stated: "This war has fully confirmed the necessity for a strong and sound merchant marine in time of peace so that it may be employed as an auxiliary of the army and navy in time of war."
Other authorities are quoted in the same article. We heard so frequently during the war, as you will recall, Mr. Chairman, of an eastern Canadian port not named but which we all knew to be Halifax. That port found itself of great use in the first world war and of inestimable value in the second world war, but in between those two wars it became a Cinderella so far as governmental activity and shipbuilding was concerned. If the government does contemplate establishing a reserve fleet and perhaps reserve shipbuilding facilities I would urge that Halifax be made the centre of that activity because of its proximity to the European continent and also because it was the base for ships which left Canada for the old country and carried cargoes through the North sea to the Archangel route. It is a port which should be greatly strengthened from both its strategic value and its natural shipbuilding advantages. Would the minister be kind enough to answer some of the questions I have asked?

My hon. friend asked a number of questions. Some of them had to do with details of the bill. The purpose of the maritime commission is to watch the interests of Canada and Canadians in shipping and to recommend such adjustments in policy to the minister as may make for the best use of a Canadian fleet for the benefit of Canada.
My hon. friend asked if we are to have a reserve fleet.. All the boats we built during the war are now actively engaged in commerce and as long as they are required in commerce I presume they will be active. If they are not required in commerce it will, I presume, be the function of the commission to advise

Maritime Commission

the government on questions such as setting up a reserve fleet, but that is a matter of policy which will be decided in due course by the government of the day, with the advise of the maritime commission.
My hon. friend said that shipbuilding costs a great deal more in Canada than in other countries. Our yards seem to be having no great difficulty in competing with the world in building ships at the present time. They are building ships for Brazil, Holland, France and, if I am not mistaken, for Portugal, and I believe that there is a very good prospect that we may be building ships for Argentina. Our shipbuilding is wholly competitive and, all things taken into account, it operates at a lower cost than obtains in United States yards.
Their yards are subsidized, are they not?

I do not know. Ours are not. So far as the United Kingdom yards are concerned, they may be able to build ships cheaper than we can, but they are booked up for the next three or four years, and if anyone wants a ship he finds that Canadian yards suit his purpose very well. Whether in the future it will be sound government policy for Canada to subsidize certain shipping routes, as is now done with certain inland routes is a matter which the maritime commission will study, and upon which it will advise the government.
As to whether any policy should be devised to stimulate shipbuilding, that is a matter for study by the maritime commission and advice to the government of the day. The maritime commission should be wholly familiar with all the requirements of Canada's maritime fleet and familiar with the government's needs in shipping and shipbuilding. It should weigh the two and be in a position to give sound advice. It will be the one agency of government whose duty it will be to examine every detail of maritime matters, shipping, and shipbuilding and to keep itself fully informed on the situation in Canada and in other parts of the world, and be in a position to answer any question which the government may require to have answered.

Would1 the minister
amplify his statement, "We do feel, however, that a merchant navy adequate to our needs should be retained." Would he explain exactly what the government had in mind when he made that statement?

That means adequate to our needs from time to time. I am not suggesting any policy; I am not in a position to do so. I would not suggest that we have a merchant 
navy sufficient to carry all our exports. I would suggest that we require a merchant navy able to carry a substantial part of our exports and to protect Canada's position in the matter of freight rates and other problems of carriage. Today we are the fourth maritime nation in the world', and when the boats now on British register are returned we shall probably be the third maritime nation in the world. Whether Canada in the future will require to maintain that position is a question for the maritime commission to study, so that it will be in a position to advise the government. Being a shipping and shipbuilding nation at the moment, it is important that we shall remain a shipping and shipbuilding nation.
What about the intergovernmental maritime consultative organization?

That is a conference of interested governments formed to consider establishing an intergovernmental maritime organization. It met first in London and then in Washington, and is meeting at the present time in one of the Scandinavian countries, I think Sweden. It is discussing the present and future position of shipping; whether the present tonnage afloat is sufficient to meet the requirements; and, in general, all matters affecting world shipping. As I understand the functions, they are wholly advisory. Canada has been represented at the meetings and intends to continue as a member of that body.

In his statement the minister mentioned merchant seamen. I am wondering whether they come under the commission and, if the commission takes over, will parliament have a chance to discuss with the minister the different regulations in regard to the training of these merchant seamen? At present we have a school at St. Margaret's bay, and I imagine that that would come under this commission. Am I right in that?
No.
The school at St. Margaret's bay is no longer in existence.
When did it go out of existence?
Some months ago.

We are not going to have a school any longer?
Mr. CHEVRIER,: There were two training schools set up during the war, one at Prescott and one in Nova Scotia. Both have been closed down. They were established for the training of merchant seamen, engineers, stokers and so forth. Seamen are trained today in

Maritime Commission
schools. There is provision for this in Toronto and in Rimouski and in certain other parts of Canada.
Will this commission have any control over that at all?
That is a question to be dealt with when the bill is before the committee.
I do not know whether it is or not. That is something we want to know now.
I am submitting that it is.
The minister mentioned merchant seamen in his statement. Parliament should have a chance to discuss the different regulations in regard to merchant seamen.
Parliament will have every chance of discussing anything that the commission has to do with reference to seamen when the bill is before the house.

Under some of these other crown companies and boards that have been set up by parliament we find that we have no chance at all to discuss anything about them. We cannot find out much about them when we put questions on the order paper.

If my hon. friend was here when the discussion took place on the compensation for merchant seamen he was told under what headings and under what conditions the position with reference to merchant seamen could be discussed. I said that they could be discussed on at least' two or three occasions. I do not want to anticipate what is in the bill, but I think there will be a further opportunity at that time.

I think the minister will have to agree with me that quite often a minister has said that we could discuss a certain question at such and such a time, but when that time comes along we are politely told that we cannot. I wondered whether we could be put straight on this.
Mr. Chairman-
I should like an answer.
I have answered to the best of my ability every question that my hon. friend asked. I cannot go beyond that.
Will this commission be responsible to parliament? Can we ask questions in regard to the commission when the Minister of Transport is before the committee?

The commission will be responsible to the minister. It is a corporate body which will be set up in the nature of the national harbours board. It will be a corporate body which can be sued and can sue. The actions of the body can be discussed from time to time.
What jurisdiction has it over merchant seamen?

At the present time merchant seamen are governed by the Canada Shipping Act and under the regulations of the Department of Labour. It may or may not be that at some future time the maritime commission may take over certain functions which are at present under these two jurisdictions. There is nothing in the legislation which specifies that the maritime commission will have direct charge of merchant seamen.

I am sure that all shipping and seafaring men will be anxious to see what the bill contains. They will appreciate this resolution which establishes a corporation to be known as the Canadian maritime commission. We need to coordinate, correlate and consolidate all matters pertaining to merchant shipping. This is something which should have been done long ago, and I welcome this resolution. I am not going to speak at any length on it because I want to see what is in the bill. I wish to say that at one time the township of Yarmouth owned more shipping per capita than any other place in the world. At one time Canada was a country to be very much considered when it came to world shipping and I should like to see her in that position again. This is a step in the right direction without any question. I just wish to say that I heartily endorse the resolution.

I have a question or two to ask on the principle of the bill, that is, if there is any principle in it. The resolution states that the Canadian maritime commission is:
... To exercise certain powers and perform certain duties and functions under the Canada Shipping Act. to administer any steamship subvention voted by parliament. . . .
Will all subsidies and subventions, which are one and the same thing, be under the control of the Canadian maritime commission?
Yes.

That will make for a lot less work for quite a few of the departments. For instance, all the subsidies paid by the Department of Public Works will come under the maritime commission?
Maritime Commission
We do not refer to ferry boats as shipping.
Some of them are not because they do not float.
The subsidies under the Department of Public Works which go to the ferries and the different boats are not classed as subsidies under shipping?
Not the subsidies under the Public Works Act.
Under Trade and Commerce?
Yes.
And under Transport?
Yes.

Here is a chance for the ministers in these departments to have a lot less work to do. These matters will all be administered under the Canadian maritime commission. I am not going to go into the details of this resolution, but I should1 like to know if all the subventions and subsidies which are to be expended by this commission will be put in the estimates and then handed over to the commission and the commission be not responsible to any minister.
It will be responsible to the Minister of Transport.

The Minister of Reconstruction mentioned some very large ship building plants in Canada, and I should like to ask him, if it is relevant to the resolution, to tell us where the largest privately owned shipyards in Canada are located.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not relevant to the resolution.
My first impulse would be to say Canadian Vickers in Montreal, but I am not sure.
I have nothing more to say at the present time, but when the bill is before us we may get some information with regard to subsidies.

The minister has not
answered certain questions I asked. First, will the commission have anything to do with rates? Second, will the commission have power to direct traffic through Canadian ports?

Ocean rates, I should judge, are fixed by competition. The maritime commission might fix rates and find that the ships could not operate under them. The answer

is that ocean-going rates will not be fixed by the maritime commission. As far as inland rates go, adjudication is the function of the board of transport commissioners.
What about the question of directing traffic through Canadian ports? Will the commission have power in that regard?
No. The shipbuilding industry is a private industry and I presume ships will go where the traffic offers. Usually it is traffic that attracts ships and not vice versa.

I have just a few observations to make on this resolution. Last year I supported the proposal for a Canadian maritime commission and I was not alone; I had the support of the late member for Halifax. Now it is the intention of the government to increase the powers of that commission by placing all steamships subsidies voted by parliament under the administration of the commission. Those subsidies were granted by the Department of Trade and Commerce and I desire to pay tribute to Mr. F. E. Bawden, who has retired but had been there for a long time. He was very helpful to members of parliament whenever they needed his assistance in establishing the amount of the subsidy.
I believe, sir, that all subsidies should be under the control or administration, not of a commission, but of a competent civil servant responsible to the minister, who, in turn, should be responsible to the house. Perhaps I am old-fashioned. Perhaps I am too old a member of parliament to be sufficiently streamlined in my views, but that is my conception .of parliamentary responsibility. I am strongly opposed to any commission that will dispose of moneys voted by parliament. The minister is responsible to the house, and the minister never had any trouble about subsidies. Sometimes there was a little discussion but everything was in order, and while members of the opposition looked at the estimates through magnifying glasses they found no scandal. Some subsidies were given to large companies like the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; others were given to maritime companies that were doing excellent service.
This proposal with regard to the commission is one step further in increasing bureaucracy. I may be wrong, but this is a matter of principle with me. I do not know those who are in charge of subsidies at the present time, not

Maritime Commission
in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, but in the Department of Trade and Commerce. They may be competent, but if they are not competent the minister should replace them with competent people. No one will convince me that there are no civil servants who can do the work. I would suggest to the minister that he amend the resolution and replace the commission with the same men he has in view for administering the service, but no commission. That is the first point.
The second point is this:
Provision is made further for the advisory functions of the commission, for the employment of professional and technical advisers and assistants and the remuneration thereof-
Oh, the remuneration thereof. That is important. It goes with technicality and profession.

and for all expenses under the act to be paid out of moneys appropriated by parliament for the purpose.
What the department needs in this regard is not so much professional men and technicians as plain common-sense men with experience. The trouble in all departments at present-and I waited for an occasion to say this-is that there are too many technicians and too many professional men. Most civil servants do not want to start at the bottom and go up quietly, learning from experience every year. They come out of universities as geniuses ready to govern the whole world, and they are too bright and. clever for our time. They give the cold shoulder to those who have been there for a long time, who know their business, who have experience, and who are not so competent because they have not so many letters after their names.
The hon. gentleman is perfectly right,

Thank you. In other times, what was needed of civil servants was intelligence, common sense and a good high school education and they were ready to learn. Now they do not want to learn. They are ready to teach, and that is the trouble, and they teach us a great lesson, the lesson of incompetence. I remember, in the old times when Jim Malcolm was Minister of Trade and Commerce, there was a small company organized at Riviere du Loop to operate a ferry service between Riviere du Loup, Tadoussac and St. Simeon, which is one of the finest services of the kind in Canada. In those days the thing to do was to see the minister, and if he felt that the service was needed he told' us to go and see Mr. F. E. Bawden, who was a nice old gentleman with experience. He would tell
us what were the requirements for passengers and traffic and what the department could do. He had experience and everything was done in a familiar way. Nothing was said against him in former times, because he was doing his work very well.
I do not criticize those who are in charge now; I do not know them. I simply say that the old practice was an excellent one. There is something much more important about the Canadian maritime commission, and that is that, in the first place, we should have a Canadian merchant marine. We had a big navy during the war. Very well. Now that we are in the post-war period1, we need a big merchant marine, and last session I made suggestions accordingly to the railway and shipping committee when I inquired about Park Steamships.
The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply and the Minister of Transport are two of the best and most active ministers in the cabinet. I may say the same thing about another one who will be closely related to them under this legislation, namely, the Minister of Trade and Commerce; and this is not to depreciate the other ministers. I speak of one thing, the Canadian maritime commission. I believe that we should have kept all the ships we had during the war, and that Canada should have her own bottoms for shipping Canadian goods throughout the world. Why should we be dependent on any other country for that? I have been told, although I am not sure about it, that the Greek firm of Goulandris offered to buy quite a number of Canadian ships, and they are waiting for a short time longer to put the Greek flag on those ships. I wonder if that is true. I should like to have some information about that.
At the present time, ships are just as precious to the country as are railways or aeroplanes. We appreciate the new methods of transportation. Everything is being modernized. Nevertheless, ships will always have their place in trade. That is why I cannot say otherwise-though without any undue spirit of criticism-than that there is no need for a Canadian maritime commission at the present time, if this commission is to do part of the work actually done by the Department of Trade and Commerce. I am warning the government about the new trend toward getting so much technical advice in trade. Trade is done by a buyer and a purchaser, and Canadian tradesmen who ship their goods by water or by air and who may require information, get it mostly from the bureau of statistics, although they may get some information from those who have been in the depart-
Maritime Commission

ment for a long time. The dealings of trade must be carried on by two people or by two companies, the seller and the buyer. Nothing can be changed about that. That principle cannot be streamlined. When there is a third party, it causes embarrassment to the other two. This is no criticism; it is a warning.
I believe that trade is the lifeblood of this country and we cannot play with it. We must keep the largest possible number of ships. We should build ships for Canada instead of building them for any other country or selling our own ships. I remember that in 1937, on the eve of the war, I went to England and visited the Clyde. What was I told by Scottish and English shippers? I was told that the maritime trade of England had gone down precisely because England had built too many ships for foreign countries. This is a warning. At the time I remember that the newspapers of Edinburgh and Glasgow were repeating the same thing constantly. What I say now is what I read then. It seems to me that it does not serve any purpose to recall facts which are positively true and it does not serve any purpose either to recall the experience of other countries. If Great Britain had built ships for herself instead of building them for other countries, her position in world trade would have been much better on the eve of the war and Germany could not have controlled the trade of many other countries.
I will just leave it at that, and I warn the minister seriously about this problem which I consider to be of the utmost importance, the problem of Canada having the largest possible number of ships, selling Canadian ships to no one except a Canadian and having Canadian ships registered in Canada. Why does the Canadian Pacific Railway Company register ships in London and elsewhere? Why does it not register its ships in Canada? What is the use of having our own legislation about shipping if it is not taken advantage of by the biggest shipping company in the country and which calls itself a Canadian company? It is for the protection of our own trade and for the protection of the Canadian people that I am so emphatic about this. I do not want the Canadian maritime commission. I do not believe in it. I want the control of shipping under parliament. That is all I want.

I have been trying to catch your eye, Mr. Chairman, for about twenty minutes. I desire to ask the minister a question or two. For about fifty years there has been a passenger and cargo steamer service on the inland lakes of British Columbia, some ships carrying passengers and cargo and
some carrying cargo only. Throughout the years, organizations representing farmers, commercial and business interests, have urged that those steamers be brought under the board of railway commissioners and, more recently, under the board of transport commissioners, but so far without success. My understanding is that the board of transport commissioners at the present time have control of passenger rates and freight tariffs but do not have any control over schedules or services given on those inland lakes, with respect to either passenger or freight service. That has been a great handicap to producers in that district for many years, because many of them depend on the steamer service for getting their produce to market. Even last year carloads of apples were taken down the Arrow lakes on a barge pulled by a tug supplied by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, after the weather was nearly at zero. Hundreds of tons of baled hay stood in the open on the wharves, because the accommodation supplied by the small barge, taking one carload on it at a time and making two or three trips a week, simply could not handle the product in the time required. I myself saw a whole carload of hay standing on the wharf and it had been there for nearly three weeks waiting for transportation. In view of the fact that this resolution says:
That it is expedient to present a bill to establish a corporation to be known as the Canadian maritime commission to exercise certain powers and perform certain duties and functions under the Canada Shipping Act, to administer any steamship subvention voted by parliament, and to exercise powers or perform duties and functions under any other act or order of the governor in council.
I wish to ask the minister this question. At the present time I understand the postal department pays a subsidy to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for carrying the mails on these lakes. In view of the fact that through the years it has been impossible to get these steamers brought under the board of railway commissioners, or more recently, the board of transport commissioners, will these steamers be brought under the control of the maritime commission, in view of the terms of the resolution?

I presume that, in order to answer the hon. gentleman, one would have to have the bill before him. However I can tell him that the resolution, in its present wording, would not cover a position such as the one to which he refers. The Transport Act was amended last year in order to do that. While I am not familiar with the locality he has in mind and cannot answer

the question which he asks, I can say that it is not the purpose of this resolution to deal with that situation.
Thank you.

If it is not out of order, I should like to ask the minister whether the three commissioners are to be full-time men or just part-time men. How are they to be chosen? For instance, is a labour man to be chosen, one with experience in shipbuilding; or will one be chosen from the Pacific coast, one from the Atlantic coast and one from central Canada.

There is no provision in the bill specifying how the commission will be appointed. There will be three full-time commissioners, and they will be appointed by the governor in council. But what system the government may adopt, if any, will be determined by the government.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Howe thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 336, to establish the Canadian maritime commission.

Mr. Chairman, the North Battleford agricultural society held a fat-stock show and sale in May of this year. Some of that beef found its way here to the city of Ottawa. I saw an advertisement in one of the local papers advertising the North Battleford beef. I went to the store which had advertised, and said I wanted to get some good beefsteak. When I asked for that North Battleford beef I was shown a piece of beef which certainly was not of choice quality. I protested and said I did not think that could be show beef, whereupon the manager of the store, hearing, the discussion, came along, went to the cooler and brought out a piece of choice beef.
I bring this matter up because I believe, when these meats are offered for sale in butcher shops, and held out as show beef, there should be some means of identification for the protection of the buyer and that of the producer. Has the minister or his department any means of identifying beef by marking, or in some other way, for the protection of the consumer and the producer?
Right Hon, J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture): So far as I know, there is no
practical way of checking that, except in the way it was checked by the hon. member. When he saw an advertisement and went in to buy a certain thing, he saw that he got it. Apparently that is what the hon. member did in this case. Stores do advertise things for sale, and do sell other things. If one goes in and asks for beef he is likely to get only beef; but if he says he wants a particular kind he will probably get that kind. So far as I know, there is no other protection.

Then there is nothing to stop a butcher from buying one carcass of choice beef and then selling perhaps ten or fifteen carcasses. There would seem to be no great difficulty to have some way of branding beef as a special type. The butcher will charge nine or ten cents a pound more for the choice beef, and I should think it would be simple to identify it from the time it leaves the farm until it is sold to the customer.

I should like to say a word on this item. I believe when it was last considered there was a good deal of discussion concerning beef. The people in, my constituency are not at all satisfied with respect to the situation in connection with beef, and are greatly concerned about the loss of the United States market. They envisage a time when we shall be left without that market, and when the beef situation will deteriorate seriously.
I do not propose to enter into a detailed discussion on this matter, because I understand the whole question was taken up in considerable detail the other day. The minister assured the house that he was taking care of the United States meat market, and that it will be there for us when the time comes that we have taken care of Britain's needs. I understand that assurance was given by the minister. I appreciate it, and congratulate him upon it. I hope he will be strong, enough in the cabinet and in the country to see that that assurance is made good.
Meanwhile the people who produce beef in my constituency have told me they consider that the minister should take steps to increase meat production in Canada, which they believe he could do to the point where we could take care of Britain's needs and also provide a surplus to hold the United States market. The people in my constituency say that it is just a matter of price; that if the price of beef is taken care of the production will increase to a point sufficient to supply all the needs.
The minister may feel he has done all he can up to the present time to increase beef production. The best informed men in my
Supply-Agriculture

constituency do not believe that is so. I do not attempt to speak with authority in the matter, although those closely connected with me are engaged in the production of beef and probably know a good deal about it. Men in my constituency who, I am sure, do know, are satisfied that if the minister changed his policy in connection with beef we could supply Great Britain's needs, and also the United-States market.
I now turn to the matter of hog production. Again the people in my constituency who produce hogs are dissatisfied' with the situation. Mine is one of the major hog producing constituencies. When the minister had a suitable price for hog production during the war we saw hogs in all directions in my constituency, but now one has to look many miles to see any hogs. Men who have allowed their hog producing facilities to fail off are hardheaded and practical men, men who know whether or not money can be made in the production of hogs; men who know when the hog situation is precarious and when it is stable. These men have gone out of the production of hogs for purely business reasons.
I do not propose to try to suggest to the minister the details -of what is necessary; but once more the difficulty arises, according to what they tell me, from the fact that the prices they have to pay for the things which enter into the production of hogs and the prices they get for the finished hog show unsuitable relationship. Then there is the fact that the income tax collector takes away a considerable amount of what is gained through the production of hogs. When those three items are considered' they say it simply is not worth while to produce hogs.
They point also to the fact that there is a lack of stability in the hog situation; that there is no assurance that the price of hogs will not suddenly go out just when they have sows and other facilities to produce hogs in considerable supply. Therefore they will be the loser or, to use a common expression, they will be left holding the bag. I am not criticizing the minister and I want him to understand that fully. I d-o not want to be harsh about the matter at all, because I realize that the minister is not master in his own department; that at times he must defer to the opinions of other men in the cabinet; that sometimes those men do- not know nearly as much about agriculture as they ought to know.
I just want to say this in strengthening the minister's hands in striking out for a better situation with regard to hog production. Men in my constituency are not by any means

satisfied with the set-up with regard to hogs and if that set-up were made right, if the prices of the things which they have to feed to hogs and the price which they get after the hogs are shipped were right and if they were given a reasonable assurance .that the income tax collectors would not come around and steal a large percentage of what they had gained by their hard efforts, the minister would have a tremendous production of hogs in my constituency. I believe that would apply generally to all constituencies in western Canada.
I notice, in reading over Hansard, that the minister has said that there just is not the feed available. Perhaps there is not the feed available at this time, but I would say that the men in my constituency and in other western constituencies with whom I have talked are of the opinion that the minister could get the feed if he just had a free hand in connection with the conditions under which that feed could be produced. Once more price is an important factor. Feed could be produced. There are irrigation areas in Alberta which could be turned into the production of barley and other feeds if it were found profitable so to do. I just wanted to draw these matters to the attention of the minister so that he will know how the people of my constituency feel anyway.
I wish to turn now to sheep production. There is widespread dissatisfaction, I would say universal dissatisfaction in my constituency with the sheep policy of the Department of Agriculture. It is pointed out that the cost of producing wool and producing sheep is going up from year to year, and there are considerable risks which must be faced. The result is that men do not feel they can produce sheep with confidence and assurance. They point to conditions across the line which are much more conducive to an attitude of confidence among sheep producers. They say that if those conditions could be imitated in Canada we would have plenty of sheep and wool produced in this country.
I shall say no more with regard to that. I just wish to say in a general sort of way that now is the time to increase the production of feeds, of beef, of pork and pork products and of wool and sheep. I think this country should be turned into a perfect larder of food from coast to coast. I believe the minister agrees completely with me. It is-the duty of the Department of Agriculture to come out strongly for measures which will enable the people who are engaged in the production of these important commo-

dities to produce to the full of their capacity right now. I know the minister cannot tell of the difficulties which surround him and I realize there are many of them. However I have said what the people in my constituency think. Therefore I have discharged my responsibility as the representative of the federal riding of Lethbridge in the year 1947.

I notice in the minister's report that reference is made to farm management which comes under the economics division, and there are a few questions I wish to ask on that particular subject. On page 189 of the report reference is made to a study that is being carried on in the milk district of Winnipeg with a view to providing an analysis of costs of production. The report states that a preliminary report has been distributed to cooperators. I should like to know what is meant by the term "cooperators". Also, I should like to know if there is such a report and, if so, will it be made available to the public and when may we expect it?

The Manitoba dairy study on the central tendencies of dairy costs was carried on by the economics branch. The major value of cost accounting to any enterprise is in the fund of information that is necessary to be supplied in order to calculate the costs. This requires data on food production, labour and other details of farm management not likely to be secured otherwise. The end results in cost calculations are also valuable if only to appraise what is likely to happen under any given price situation. The central tendencies in the cost of milk production in the Winnipeg milk area were placed in a table by those who carried on the investigation. The general result is that they give a number of forms' of cost groups. In 1942-43, 104 farms were examined into; in 1943-44, 93 farms; in 1944-45, 91 farms. Those were farmers who cooperated with the economics branch in making this investigation possible. They carry on and give information as to what happens on their farms and the costs of everything related to them. Results are calculated on the experiences obtained through the cooperation of these farmers. The average cost for the first year was 73-5; for the second year, 83, and for the third year, 85-9. That is on the basis of butter fat.
I asked whether the report would be made public and if so, when we could expect it.
When the report is completed it will be made public.

In the same report there is a section dealing with land utilization, and it is stated that the land use committee met in Regina on April 5, 1945, and made certain recommendations. It states that a great deal of information is available or has been accumulated on the question of land utilization, but it is said also that this has not been effectively distributed for public use. These words appear in the minister's report:
.. .that too few persons are aware of these facts; and too little use is being made of these facts. It was felt that coordination of this information should be undertaken and a broad policy of land use developed.
That is very good advice. What is the department doing at the present time to distribute the information more effectively than has been the case in the past?

We put out reports when the investigations have been completed in connection with any districts investigated, and through those reports we distribute the information which has been gained. For example, I presume the investigation referred to about which there were discussions at Regina is something along the lines of what I have here, which says that in Saskatchewan a land classification was completed in the Elrose-Conquest area in a block of twenty municipal units in the extreme southwestern corner of the province. Such a report would be available to the persons interested and most of them would live in that area. The reports are published for distribution.
Does that mean that they are mailed in accordance with a specific mailing list to get into the hands of the people who would benefit from the report?

They are distributed free to anyone who asks for them. When an investigation of that kind is made in a district nearly everyone in the district would1 know that the investigation was going on. In the milk investigation in Manitoba, for example, when you visit and get in touch continuously with 109 farmers I would expect that all of them would ask for a copy of the report when it was made. I would presume that it would go even farther than that; that the reports would go not only to those interviewed who inquired for it but to others roundabout who knew that the investigation was going on and inquired for a copy of the report.

I might make a suggestion to the minister. I have had a little experience in adult education, and I found that one
Supply-Agriculture

of the chief obstacles arose from the fact that the people did not know that a report of that kind was available. Most people would ask for the information if they knew it was available, and where they could get it. Those who would be directly involved in the investigation would, of course, know all about it, but a great many would not know. I would suggest that reports of that type might be sent around to all the schools, perhaps with a note requesting the schoolteacher to make it known to the public in the area that such a report was available. It might then find its way into the hands of the people who would benefit from it the most.
Under "Marketing Research" in the economics division there is an account, in the annual report of the minister, of an investigation that was made and may still be under way into the marketing of fruits and vegetables in the city of Winnipeg, a study which was requested by the Manitoba department of agriculture. It is pointed out that the investigation was carried on to find out, first, the feasibility of building a wholesale terminal market in Winnipeg for the marketing of fruits and vegetables, and, second, what portion of that market could be served by Manitoba-grown vegetables and potatoes. It is further pointed out that seventeen per cent of the volume laid down in Winnipeg was of Manitoba origin and that about $9,000,000 worth of fruits, vegetables and potatoes were marketed in Winnipeg during 1944-45, which is a substantial amount. Is there a full report available of that investigation which would show what part of that product was sold in the city of Winnipeg and what portion of it was distributed to other towns in the province, together with any information along that line?

There is a report of that investigation which has been published by the Manitoba government. The investigation was asked for by the Manitoba government; the results have been made known to them, and their report has already been published.

To what extent is the department carrying on investigations to determine the cost of production of various agricultural crops? I suppose that would be carried on under this branch, and I Should like to know the various products that have been investigated and where one can get information as to their cost of production in different areas?

The only one that is being carried on at the moment is the one in Winnipeg with regard to milk costs. There is information available in regard to the three years that I mentioned. That is continuing,

the information is being brought up to date, and when that is completed the report will be published.

I w'onder why more work of that kind is not being done, if that is the only such project now being carried on. If we are to implement the principles of the Agricultural Prices Support Act the department will require information on the cost of production of a variety of agricultural products in order to be in a position to establish intelligently floor prices for the different agricultural products. I am surprised to hear the minister say that costs of production of only one product are now being investigated. The department must have information on costs of production of various farm products if it is to establish floor prices intelligently. I would ask the minister how he expects to establish reasonable floor prices without such information.

Of course for many j'ears organizations have been set up in the provinces to do this very work. To my knowledge, the economics branch of the Department of Agriculture has been doing this very type of work in Saskatchewan at least since 1914, when I first went into the legislature. The branch was there then.
That is the provincial branch?

Yes, and the gentleman in charge of that branch then has, for quite a number of years, been in charge of the branch here. I refer to Doctor Booth. He had his experience first in Saskatchewan; later went to Washington, and still later came here and has been carrying on these investigations with the cooperation of the provinces. There is one difficulty about such information. I have, for instance, a table here showing production costs as 73-5 cents for 1942-43, 83 cents for 1943-44, and 85-9 cents for 1944-45. That bears out the contention of many persons. By the time you get through with your investigations the costs have changed. While it is an advantage to know what the costs have been in the months or years that have gone by, the information is not just as valuable as one would expect in determining what costs are today. It simply gives one a method by which he can make perhaps a pretty close calculation for his own operations, but as for giving statistics that can be relied on at the time you are operating, such figures are not as helpful as they might appear on the surface.

I agree with the minister that the cost of production continually fluctuates *with the costs of the elements entering into

Supply-Agriculture
production. I know that studies have been made at various times on the cost of producing wheat and various other products on different sized farms, and the costs vary not only with the method of production but with the quantity of production. But it seems to me that the department should be carrying on a running inventory of costs of production so that it will know from time to time approximately what those costs are. I do not know whether that would be expensive.
It would be a costly operation.

But I think it is a necessary operation if we are to deal intelligently with agriculture. It could be carried on as the minister suggested, in cooperation with the provinces. It seems to me that that particular line of study was not followed very closely during the war. As a matter of fact we could not do it very well because we were too busy with a lot of other matters. It seems to me that the time has now come when the department, either by itself or in cooperation with the provincial department of agriculture, should get into that field again and determine the cost of production. It is interesting not only from the fact that it may be necessary to implement the Agricultural Prices Support Act but also to determine and to give the farmers some idea of the most economical size of unit for them to operate. There is a tremendous field of investigation in this work. It is one of the ways in which we can reduce cost of production in the country.
I would suggest to the minister that this is one place in which some expansion might be made in determining the cost of production. Certainly, if the time comes when it is necessary to implement the Agricultural Prices Support Act, unless the minister has available in the future information that will give to him some idea of what is a fair price he will have quite a time explaining to farmers that the price established is a satisfactory one. The only way he can prove it satisfactorily is by having figures on the cost of production.
