I have a few questions I should like to ask the minister in regard to this item. Is the dairy inspector who inspects the dairies that supply fluid milk, bottled milk, responsible for the price paid, or is there a standard price that should be paid according to the amount they are getting for their bottled milk, or are they allowed to buy it at whatever price they can get it?

In so far as the distribution of milk is concerned, as has been stated quite a number of times on the floor of the house-and the last time I remember it was under discussion was a year ago when the hon. member for Haldimand, who, I am sure, we are all sorry is not with us during the discussion, brought out the fact that when this question was investigated at the time of the prices board investigation-it was demonstrated that all matters such as have been referred to, really come under provincial control. The milk boards of the provinces have control over that matter. Investigations with regard to prices are carried on by the provinces or by the local people in some . community where they have a board in charge, but not by Ottawa.

I should like to ask the minister a question about laboratory assistants. There were three last year. They are now done away with and three assistant technicians have been appointed. Are these the same people just receiving an increase in salary? Can the minister tell us something about that?
It is a change in the title.
And an advance in salary.
Yes.
Before the item carries, I should like to ask a question about the production of cheese thus far this year as compared with the production in 1944, 1945 and 1946.

The cheese production in Canada for May, 1946, was 17,000,000 pounds, and for May, 1947, 12,225,000 pounds. The change is downward; it was 28-1 per cent for May. From January to May the production for 1946 was 30,245,000 pounds, and for 1947, 22,830,000 pounds, or a decrease of 24-5 per cent. Of course I think it will be readily agreed that probably it is too early in the season to compare one year with another. It will be noted from these figures that nearly all the production was in May, and there is some question as to whether May was a favourable month for production for this year as was May a year ago. The season is some weeks late this year all across Canada in connection with all production. But I think we would have to be pretty well through June and probably into July before
Supply-Agriculture

we could make a comparison which would indicate clearly just where we are going in that production.

Is the minister optimistic enough to think there is to be as much production this year as there was last, in view of the fact there are so many cheese factories closed in eastern Ontario. How many cheese factories have been closed in the eastern counties over the past year or two?
There is no indication at the moment that we are likely to be quite as high in our production this year as we were last year.
The minister has not answered the question as to how many cheese factories have been closed in the eastern counties over the past two years.

I am sorry, but I shall not be able to give them for eastern Ontario. I can give the figures for Ontario. They are not broken down into eastern and western Ontario. The number of cheese factories in 1943, 1944 and 1945-there is nothing later than that; I am sorry, but I shall not be able to give them for the last year-were as follows: in 1943, 561; in 1944, 556; in 1945, 547. I have been given to understand that the decrease has been running at about that rate through 1946 and 1947, but the number of cheese factories is not the complete answer. As is known, since 1939 we have been paying subsidies to encourage the enlargement and improvement of cheese factories. In some instances you have two converted into one; that is, two closed up and one of a larger type opened up and better equipped, so that the decrease as to numbers would not entirely show the picture.

I think the minister will agree that the decrease in the amount of cheese produced has been just about on a ratio with the number of cheese factories closed. Most of that has been due to the low price of milk for cheese purposes. A lot of milk has been going to the larger cities in the whole milk trade in view of the larger price obtainable for that milk.
Another question is this. In view of the fact that our cheese has been going to the old country in the same form for the last fifty years, 90-pound cheddars, and marked there as an empire product instead of as a Canadian product, and also in view of the fact the New Zealand cheese is going there in small attractive packages, has this government made

an attempt to have the exporters from this country make our cheese a little more attractive to the English consumer?

That was one of the efforts made when we did pay the subsidy, to have cheese made up in some factories in a form different from that in which it had been made before. One idea was to standardize the forms in which the cheese was pressed in order to produce cheese more acceptable in form. In addition to that, during the war we carried on investigations as to possible coverings of cheese, cheesecloth, which would make possible the marking of cheese, and today we have cheese going to Britain completely marked with the name "Canada" to distinguish it from what is generally known as empire cheese. That work is being done now as effectively as possible, but it has been completed only within the last few months.
Is it sold under Canadian auspices in England or sold by British commission men and still sold as empire cheese even though it is marked Canadian?

You cannot sell anything in Britain today as anything but a food board product. They do not permit the Danes or anyone else to put up an advertising sign in the country. As a matter of fact, they are all pulled down. People cannot go and ask for any particular kind of any particular food, and the reason is obvious. The food board has great difficulty in securing sufficient food for the people of Britain, and therefore it has entirely ruled out the possibility of people going to a shop and saying they want a particular commodity, whether Canadian cheese or Canadian bacon or Danish cheese or Danish bacon. They simply go and ask for cheese or bacon and they get whatever food the ministry can provide them with. There is no possibility of getting it delivered as anything else.
But advertising is not all done on a printed basis. A lot of it is done by word of mouth, and if someone is not fighting for or boosting Canadian cheese, something can be done in that direction.
The product is distributed in Britain by the ordinary merchant and he has to take what he gets.

We are looking forward to the day when that situation will be changed and we may be able to advertise Canadian cheese. We want people to know what Canadian cheese tastes like.

Supply-Agriculture

In connection with the production of dairy products, it would be interesting if the minister could tell us the production of butter in 1946 for the same months as in 1947, just as in the case of cheese.
Creamery butter in May, 1946, was 31,864,000 pounds and, the production for May, 1947, is 31,269,000 pounds. That is, it is down by 1-9 per cent, or almost two per cent.
Does the Canadian government maintain storage facilities in England for Canadian products, or do we turn over Canadian products to the British food board at the Canadian seaboard?

The British food department takes delivery of all our food products at the Canadian port. That was the arrangement made during the war because they assumed all responsibility for shipping, and that has continued. I should have given the figure for the entire period from January to May in 1946 and 1947. It was 81,753,000 pounds for 1946 and 82,563,000 pounds for 1947, which is an increase of about one per cent over the whole period.
Can the minister explain how there is an increase in butter of approximately one per cent and yet a decrease in the manufacture of cheese of twenty-eight per cent in the same month this year?

It is largely explained by what was mentioned a few moments ago, that probably the greater part of the fluid milk comes out of areas where cheese was originally produced1. That may be due to the fact that the cheese area extends from about Three Rivers in Quebec to Ingersoll in Ontario, and all the large cities in Canada are in that area. There is a much larger urban population in that section than in any other, and therefore fluid milk would be taken from those districts to the cities. Much of our butter is produced in western Canada where the population is not nearly as dense as it is in the eastern part and where we do not produce cheese in any event. For that reason the variation will be greater in cheese when you take out the fluid milk.
Can the minister give particulars as to the situation in the manufacture of butter in May, 1946, and May, 1947, in Ontario so that we can make a comparison?

In 1946, in May, the figure is 7.986,000 pounds, and in 1947, 8,259,000 pounds. That is, butter production is up there. From January through it is also up
considerably. Cheese production in Ontario through the whole area is down and cheese production is down through the whole period from January to May, which, of course, does not bear out the suggestion I was making; nevertheless the cheese is not made anywhere else except in that district. I am quite sure therefore, that the cheese reduction itself is due largely to milk goinig as fluid milk. It is not due to the fact that it is going to that extent into butter.

But if that were so with regard to cheese, would it not be equally so with regard to butter? It seems to me that there is quite an alarming reduction in the manufacture of cheese, particularly in Ontario this year, and that is reflected across Canada by the great decrease in the export of cheese overseas. That being the case, I think it is time, for the sake of the cheese producer in Canada, for the Department of Agriculture to be greatly concerned with the retrograde movement of an industry that is important to Canada. The hon. member for Brant asked certain questions about the advertising of Canadian cheese and the marking of that cheese overseas. Now that the war has been over for two years, and in view of the fact that cheesemaking is a fundamental industry to a great number of farmers who have not the same access to city markets as others, I suggest that the time has come for the department to give serious attention to the cheese industry in Canada and to foster the production of this commodity in every way possible. The facts revealed tonight in that regard are alarming.

On the question of advertising, the British will not permit us to advertise at all. We had a large advertising programme on in the last few years before the war. We started it in 1936 and built it up to 1939, but we are not permitted to advertise there at present. The only means of getting advertising there is through news items. The discussion we are having tonight may appear in the newspapers and, if it does, we shall get advertising to that extent. Otherwise we are not allowed to advertise there.
On the other question I should repeat what I said earlier in the discussion. Cheese production is a month late this year because of the nature of the season. That in itself largely accounts for the fact that cheese is down as compared with butter. My hon, friend shakes his head, but I have heard him use the argument time after time since he has been here in the house that price has something to do with this. Everyone admits
Supply-Agriculture

that cheese is higher in price than butter at the present time, and much higher. If price is the only thing that counts, or the return that the farmer can get for it, then cheese production should certainly be higher. But everyone who knows anything about farming in Ontario knows the production season is at least a month late. A month or a month and a half from now we could make a much more valuable comparison than we can at the present time.
Will the minister state what surplus of butter we have at the present time as compared with what we had a year ago?

Before the minister rises to answer, may I ask him to tell us if the Canadian government has made any representation to the British parliament asking them to permit the advertising of Canadian cheese?

We know better than to make that representation, because we are told regularly that we cannot d'o so. We have the United Kingdom government's representatives here in Ottawa all the time. As a matter of fact they live in the same building as I do and I see them regularly. We know we cannot advertise is Britain at the present time.
The minister might go a little farther and state that for a number of years we have not been allowed to advertise.
Since the war.
The minister made the statement that it was only because of the late season there was less cheese production this year.	t
I said that was the main reason.

I should like to remind the minister that it is unlikely that as much cheese could be produced with fewer cheese factories in this country; therefore it is not just the late season which has caused the smaller production of cheese.
A question was asked about storage. On June 1, 1947, the amount in stock was 23,533,331 pounds of butter; and a year ago on the same date the amount was 18,226,957 pounds.

While we are talking about the production of cheese and the closing of factories, may I say that in eastern Ontario last year-and that is not taking into account the month of May-twenty-three cheese factories closed up. Very few of those cheese factories amalgamated, and where they were amal-

gamated there was little influence on production because of the long haul to bring the milk to the cheese factory. A number of these factories have gone into other forms of processed milk. So there is no other reason than that for the production of cheese being cut down in eastern Canada. We cannot expect to get as much production when we have twenty-three cheese factories less. I know of several more factories which closed this spring; and several of them, instead of making Cheddar cheese, have gone into making other forms of cheese.
Will the minister say how much increase there has been in powdered or concentrated milk? Some of our factories in Perth county are closed and some of them are milk powder factories.

On condensed milk,
there is 3,104,000 pounds for May, 1946, and 2,801,000 pounds for May, 1947, or a decrease of 9-8 per cent. On the whole period from January to May, the decrease has been a little greater, namely, 10-9 per cent. On evaporated milk the decrease is 0-4 per cent for the month and the increase is 1-8 per cent for the period. On whole milk powder there is a decrease of 3-9 per cent in the month of May and an increase of 6-6 per cent for the whole period from January to May inclusive.

Much has been said about the number of cheese factories being closed. We have had the viewpoints from various members. I should like to have a statement from the minister himself as to the explanation.
I have given it twice, and I think that is enough for one night.

May I just say to the minister that I hope he will bring strong representations to. bear on the British government with respect to our advertising our own products. In Canada it is true that we are attentive to the possibility for the future, as well as for the present, of the British consumer of our agricultural products. It surely cannot be said that we are not entitled to advertise our own agricultural products in Great Britain. I can understand the viewpoint of the government there when they say they do not wish to encourage more consumption because they have not more to give to their people. At the same time, if you read any British magazine or journal you will find advertised many things which are in short supply. When we supply these foodstuffs largely, if not entirely, at our own expense, at the present time, I find it difficult to under-

House oj Commons
stand why we should be dictated to by the United Kingdom government. As a Canadian, I resent it. I feel that the minister should do everything possible to make sure that we establish our brands for a time when conditions may be more competitive than they are today.

Representations have been made by the Ontario cheese producers' association from time to time. Would the minister state if tihose representations have been implemented as far as possible by his department?

Most of the discussions we have had with the cheese producers have been with regard to price, and the negotiations that we have had with Britain have established the price under the contract. We have, of course, not been able to secure as much as any producer I know of thinks he would like to have. Cheese producers are no exception. We have, however, discussed the matter fully with them, and I think they have finally agreed that we are getting all we can expect to get under the circumstances.
